vce-bio34-nucleic-acid-structure: bio34a1-nas-1
Which combination correctly describes the components of a single DNA nucleotide?
A phosphate group, a ribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
A phosphate group, a deoxyribose sugar and a nitrogenous base
An amino group, a deoxyribose sugar and a carboxyl group
Two phosphate groups, a deoxyribose sugar and uracil
A DNA nucleotide consists of a phosphate group, the pentose sugar deoxyribose and one of four nitrogenous bases (A, T, C or G). Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides, not DNA.
bio34a1-nas-2
A sample of double-stranded DNA from a native Australian frog contains 22% guanine. What percentage of the bases in this sample are thymine?
By complementary base pairing, G = C = 22%, so G + C = 44%. The remaining 56% is A + T, and since A = T, thymine is 28%. 56% is the combined A + T value, not thymine alone.
bio34a1-nas-3
Adjacent nucleotides within one strand of DNA are joined by
hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
peptide bonds formed by condensation reactions.
phosphodiester bonds between the sugar of one nucleotide and the phosphate of the next.
disulfide bridges between nitrogenous bases.

The sugar-phosphate backbone is held together by covalent phosphodiester bonds linking the 3′ carbon of one sugar to the 5′ phosphate of the next nucleotide. Hydrogen bonds join the two strands to each other, not nucleotides within a strand.
bio34a1-nas-4
Which feature is found in RNA but not in DNA?
The base uracil
A sugar-phosphate backbone
The base cytosine
Nucleotides joined in a 5′ to 3′ direction
RNA contains uracil in place of thymine. Both DNA and RNA have a sugar-phosphate backbone, contain cytosine and are built in the 5′ to 3′ direction.
bio34a1-nas-5
Two DNA fragments are the same length. Fragment X has 60% G–C base pairs and fragment Y has 35% G–C base pairs. When both are heated, which outcome is most likely?
Fragment Y separates into single strands at a higher temperature because it has more base pairs.
Both fragments separate at the same temperature because they are the same length.
Fragment Y separates at a higher temperature because A–T pairs form three hydrogen bonds.
Fragment X separates into single strands at a higher temperature because G–C pairs form three hydrogen bonds.

G–C pairs are held by three hydrogen bonds while A–T pairs are held by two, so DNA rich in G–C needs more energy (a higher temperature) to separate. Length is equal here, so base composition decides it.
bio34a1-nas-6
Explain what is meant by the statement that the two strands of a DNA molecule are 'antiparallel'. (2 marks)
The two strands run in opposite directions; one strand runs 5′ to 3′ while its complementary strand runs 3′ to 5′ (the 5′ phosphate end of one strand lies opposite the 3′ hydroxyl end of the other).
bio34a1-nas-7
One strand of a DNA segment reads 5′-ATGCCGTT-3′. Write the complementary DNA strand, labelling its 5′ and 3′ ends, and state the type of bond that holds the two strands together. (2 marks)
Complementary strand: 3′-TACGGCAA-5′ (equivalently written 5′-AACGGCAT-3′); the strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
bio34a1-nas-8
Compare the structure and role of mRNA and tRNA. (3 marks)

Both are single-stranded RNA polymers made of ribonucleotides containing ribose and A, U, C, G; mRNA is a linear molecule that carries a copy of the genetic instructions (codons) from the DNA to the ribosome; tRNA folds into a cloverleaf shape held by internal base pairing, carries an anticodon at one end and a specific amino acid at the 3′ end, delivering amino acids to the ribosome during translation.
vce-bio34-nas-c1
A virus's genome is analysed: 24% A, 31% U, 25% G and 20% C. The genome is most likely:
Double-stranded RNA
Double-stranded DNA
Single-stranded RNA
Single-stranded DNA
Uracil means RNA. In a double strand, A would equal U and G would equal C; here they do not, so it is single-stranded.
vce-bio34-transcription-and-rna-processi: bio34a1-trp-1
During transcription in a eukaryotic cell, RNA polymerase
binds to the start codon and reads the coding strand 5′ to 3′.
binds to the promoter and synthesises RNA in the 5′ to 3′ direction using the template strand.
joins Okazaki fragments to form a continuous pre-mRNA strand.
requires a primer before it can add the first ribonucleotide.

RNA polymerase binds to the promoter upstream of the gene, unwinds the DNA and adds complementary ribonucleotides to the 3′ end of the growing RNA, reading the template strand 3′ to 5′. Start codons are recognised by ribosomes in translation, not by RNA polymerase.
bio34a1-trp-2
The template strand of a DNA segment reads 3′-TACGGATTC-5′. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
5′-ATGCCTAAG-3′
3′-AUGCCUAAG-5′
5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′
5′-UACGGAUUC-3′
mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template strand, with U replacing T: template 3′-TACGGATTC-5′ gives mRNA 5′-AUGCCUAAG-3′. Option A contains thymine, so it is DNA, not RNA.
bio34a1-trp-3
Which modification of pre-mRNA protects the mRNA from degradation at its 3′ end and helps its export from the nucleus?
Addition of a poly-A tail
Addition of a methyl-guanine cap
Removal of exons by the spliceosome
Addition of a signal peptide
A poly-A tail (a long chain of adenine nucleotides) is added to the 3′ end. The methyl-guanine cap is added to the 5′ end, not the 3′ end. Splicing removes introns, not exons.
bio34a1-trp-4
A gene contains 4 exons and 3 introns. Which statement about the mature mRNA produced from this gene is correct?
It contains the 3 introns only, because exons are removed during splicing.
It is always longer than the original gene because a cap and tail are added.
It can only ever contain all 4 exons in the same order.
It may contain different combinations of exons in different cells due to alternative splicing.

Introns are removed and exons are joined. Through alternative splicing, some exons may be included or excluded, so one gene can produce several mature mRNAs and therefore several proteins. Removing introns usually makes the mature mRNA much shorter than the gene.
bio34a1-trp-5

Researchers compare the length of a human gene in the genome with the length of its mature mRNA in the cytoplasm. The gene is 18 000 nucleotides long but the mature mRNA is 2400 nucleotides long. The best explanation is that
transcription stopped early because of a mutation in the promoter.
introns, which make up most of the gene, were removed from the pre-mRNA during splicing.
the mRNA was partially translated before it left the nucleus.
only the coding strand was transcribed.

Eukaryotic genes often contain long introns that are transcribed into pre-mRNA and then spliced out, leaving only the exons in mature mRNA. Translation occurs in the cytoplasm, not before export, and only the template strand is ever transcribed.
bio34a1-trp-6
Outline the three main processing steps that convert pre-mRNA into mature mRNA in a eukaryotic cell. (3 marks)

A 5′ methyl-guanine (methylated G) cap is added to the 5′ end, which protects the mRNA and helps ribosome attachment; a poly-A tail is added to the 3′ end, which protects the mRNA from degradation and aids export; introns are removed and exons are joined together by spliceosomes (splicing).
bio34a1-trp-7
Explain how alternative splicing allows the human genome of about 20 000 protein-coding genes to produce a much larger number of different proteins. (2 marks)

During splicing, different combinations of exons from the same pre-mRNA can be retained or removed; this produces different mature mRNAs from one gene, each translated into a different polypeptide, so the number of proteins exceeds the number of genes.
bio34a1-trp-8

Transcription occurs in the nucleus of a eukaryotic cell, whereas in a prokaryote transcription and translation occur together in the cytoplasm. Give one structural reason for this difference and one consequence for RNA processing. (2 marks)

Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus, so ribosomes can access mRNA as soon as it is made (eukaryotes separate transcription in the nucleus from translation in the cytoplasm); as a consequence, prokaryotic mRNA generally does not undergo splicing, capping and tailing, whereas eukaryotic pre-mRNA is processed in the nucleus before export.
vce-bio34-trp-c1
The template strand of a gene reads 3′-TAC GGA TTC-5′. The mRNA transcribed from it is:
5′-UAC GGA UUC-3′
3′-AUG CCU AAG-5′
5′-ATG CCT AAG-3′
5′-AUG CCU AAG-3′
mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template strand, with U replacing T. Read 5′ to 3′: AUG CCU AAG.
vce-bio34-translation-and-the-genetic-co: bio34a1-tgc-1
The genetic code is described as 'degenerate'. This means that
a single codon can code for more than one amino acid.
the code is the same in almost all living organisms.
most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon.
codons overlap so that one base can belong to two codons.

Degeneracy (redundancy) means that more than one codon can specify the same amino acid, e.g. GGU, GGC, GGA and GGG all code for glycine. Option B describes universality, and the code is non-overlapping.
bio34a1-tgc-2
A tRNA molecule carries the anticodon 3′-UAC-5′. Which mRNA codon does it pair with?
The anticodon pairs complementarily and antiparallel with the codon: 3′-UAC-5′ pairs with 5′-AUG-3′, the start codon for methionine. ATG contains thymine, which is not found in mRNA.
bio34a1-tgc-3
A mature mRNA has 900 nucleotides between and including the start codon and the stop codon. What is the maximum number of amino acids in the polypeptide produced?
900 nucleotides = 300 codons. The final codon is a stop codon, which does not code for an amino acid, leaving 299 amino acids (the start codon AUG codes for methionine and is counted).
bio34a1-tgc-4
During translation, which event occurs at the ribosome?
RNA polymerase adds amino acids to the growing chain.
Peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids delivered by tRNA.
Introns are removed from mRNA as it passes through the ribosome.
The mRNA is read 3′ to 5′ until a start codon is reached.

tRNAs bring specific amino acids to the ribosome, where anticodons pair with mRNA codons and peptide bonds form between adjacent amino acids by condensation. The ribosome reads mRNA 5′ to 3′, and splicing happens in the nucleus.
bio34a1-tgc-5
A point mutation changes an mRNA codon from UAU (tyrosine) to UAA. What is the most likely effect on the polypeptide?
No effect, because the genetic code is degenerate.
Tyrosine is replaced by a different amino acid at that position only.
All amino acids after the mutation are changed because the reading frame shifts.
Translation stops early, producing a shortened, likely non-functional polypeptide.
UAA is a stop codon, so this is a nonsense mutation that terminates translation early. A substitution does not shift the reading frame, which is what an insertion or deletion would do.
bio34a1-tgc-6
Describe the role of tRNA in translation. (3 marks)

Each tRNA molecule binds (is charged with) a specific amino acid at its 3′ end; it carries this amino acid to the ribosome; its anticodon pairs complementarily with the matching mRNA codon, ensuring amino acids are added in the order specified by the mRNA.
bio34a1-tgc-7

A section of mRNA reads 5′-AUG GCU UGG AAA UGA-3′. Using the codons AUG = Met, GCU = Ala, UGG = Trp, AAA = Lys and UGA = stop, state the polypeptide produced and explain why UGA does not add an amino acid. (2 marks)
Met–Ala–Trp–Lys; UGA is a stop codon, which has no matching tRNA, so a release factor binds instead and translation terminates, releasing the polypeptide.
bio34a1-tgc-8

Scientists insert a jellyfish gene into a bacterium and the bacterium produces the same jellyfish protein. Identify the property of the genetic code that makes this possible and explain your answer. (2 marks)

The genetic code is universal; the same codons code for the same amino acids in almost all organisms, so bacterial ribosomes and tRNAs translate the jellyfish codons into the same amino acid sequence.
vce-bio34-tgc-c1
Methionine has one codon (AUG) and tryptophan has one codon (UGG). How many different mRNA sequences could code for the tripeptide Met–Trp–Met?
Each amino acid here has only one codon, so only AUG UGG AUG works. For most amino acids degeneracy would allow several sequences.
vce-bio34-gene-regulation-and-the-trp-op: bio34a1-gro-1
In the trp operon of Escherichia coli, the role of tryptophan when it is abundant is to act as a
corepressor that binds to the repressor protein, allowing it to bind the operator.
inducer that removes the repressor from the operator.
transcription factor that recruits RNA polymerase to the promoter.
structural gene product that is part of the enzyme pathway.

When tryptophan levels are high, tryptophan binds to the inactive repressor, changing its shape so that it binds the operator and blocks RNA polymerase. Removing a repressor in response to a molecule describes an inducible operon such as lac, not trp.
bio34a1-gro-2
Which statement correctly distinguishes regulatory genes from structural genes?
Structural genes code for proteins that control the expression of regulatory genes.
Regulatory genes code for proteins such as repressors that control the expression of structural genes.
Regulatory genes are never transcribed, whereas structural genes are always transcribed.
Structural genes are found only in eukaryotes.

Regulatory genes (such as trpR) code for proteins that switch other genes on or off. Structural genes (such as trpE–trpA) code for proteins with other cell functions, such as enzymes. Regulatory genes are transcribed to produce their proteins.
bio34a1-gro-3
A mutation in E. coli alters the trp repressor so that it can no longer bind tryptophan. In a medium high in tryptophan, the most likely result is that
the structural genes are never transcribed.
the repressor permanently binds the operator.
the structural genes continue to be transcribed even though tryptophan is abundant.
attenuation stops working, so transcription of the leader region cannot begin.

Without bound tryptophan, the repressor stays inactive and cannot bind the operator, so RNA polymerase continues to transcribe the structural genes (attenuation may reduce, but not fully stop, transcription). The repressor could only bind the operator when tryptophan is bound.
bio34a1-gro-4
In attenuation of the trp operon, when tryptophan levels are high,
the ribosome stalls at the trp codons of the leader sequence and an antiterminator loop forms.
the repressor binds to the leader sequence of the mRNA.
RNA polymerase cannot bind to the promoter.
the ribosome moves quickly through the leader sequence, allowing a terminator hairpin (regions 3–4) to form so transcription stops.

With plenty of tryptophan-carrying tRNA, the ribosome passes the two trp codons rapidly and covers region 2, so regions 3 and 4 pair to form a terminator hairpin and RNA polymerase detaches. Stalling and antiterminator formation occur when tryptophan is low.
bio34a1-gro-5

Researchers measured the rate of trpE mRNA production in E. coli. Cells were grown without tryptophan for 30 minutes, then tryptophan was added. The rate was high for the first 30 minutes and then dropped to near zero within a few minutes. The best explanation is that
the added tryptophan acted as a corepressor and also enabled attenuation, both reducing transcription of the structural genes.
tryptophan was converted into the repressor protein.
the structural genes were deleted from the chromosome.
the cells used up all of their RNA polymerase in the first 30 minutes.

Added tryptophan binds the repressor so it blocks the operator, and high tryptophan also causes early termination by attenuation; both reduce transcription quickly. Genes are not deleted and the repressor is a protein coded by trpR, not made from tryptophan.
bio34a1-gro-6
Describe how the trp repressor controls transcription of the trp operon when tryptophan levels in the cell are low. (2 marks)

When tryptophan is low, no tryptophan binds to the repressor (coded by trpR), so the repressor stays inactive and cannot bind to the operator; RNA polymerase can therefore bind to the promoter and transcribe the structural genes that code for the enzymes that synthesise tryptophan.
bio34a1-gro-7
Explain the advantage to E. coli of regulating the trp operon rather than expressing the structural genes continuously. (2 marks)

Making tryptophan-synthesis enzymes requires energy and resources (ATP, amino acids, nucleotides); by switching off the operon when tryptophan is already available, the bacterium avoids wasting resources and can direct them to other processes such as growth and reproduction.
bio34a1-gro-8
Explain how attenuation reduces transcription of the trp operon when tryptophan is abundant, even if some RNA polymerase molecules have already begun transcribing. (3 marks)

Transcription and translation are coupled in bacteria, so a ribosome begins translating the leader (trpL) sequence while it is being transcribed; when tryptophan (and tRNA carrying tryptophan) is abundant, the ribosome moves quickly past the trp codons in region 1 and covers region 2; this allows regions 3 and 4 to pair, forming a terminator hairpin loop that causes RNA polymerase to detach before the structural genes are transcribed.
vce-bio34-gr-c1
A mutation in the trp operator stops the repressor from binding. When tryptophan levels in the cell are high:
Transcription stops, as normal
The structural genes are still transcribed, wasting energy
The repressor binds to the promoter instead
Tryptophan binds directly to the operator
Tryptophan activates the repressor, but the repressor cannot bind the mutated operator, so RNA polymerase still transcribes trpE–trpA.
vce-bio34-protein-structure-and-the-prot: bio34a1-psp-1
The primary structure of a protein is
the folding of the chain into α-helices and β-pleated sheets.
the overall three-dimensional shape of one polypeptide.
the sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain.
the arrangement of two or more polypeptides together.

Primary structure is the linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. α-helices and β-pleated sheets are secondary structure, 3D shape is tertiary structure and multiple polypeptides is quaternary structure.
bio34a1-psp-2
Which bonds or interactions are mainly responsible for maintaining the secondary structure of a protein?
Peptide bonds between R groups
Hydrogen bonds between atoms of the polypeptide backbone
Disulfide bridges between cysteine R groups only
Phosphodiester bonds between amino acids

α-helices and β-pleated sheets are stabilised by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbone. Disulfide bridges and other R-group interactions are mainly associated with tertiary structure.
bio34a1-psp-3
Haemoglobin is made of four polypeptide chains, each containing a haem group. Which level of protein structure does haemoglobin possess that a single-chain protein like myoglobin does not?
Primary
Secondary
Tertiary
Quaternary
Quaternary structure is the association of two or more polypeptide chains into one functional protein. Myoglobin is a single polypeptide, so its highest level is tertiary structure.
bio34a1-psp-4
The term 'proteome' refers to
the complete set of proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism at a particular time.
the complete set of genes in an organism.
all the amino acids available in a cell.
the region of the ribosome where proteins are made.

The proteome is the full set of proteins expressed by a cell, tissue or organism at a given time under given conditions. The complete set of genes is the genome. Unlike the genome, the proteome varies between cell types and over time.
bio34a1-psp-5
An enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium retains its activity at 85 °C, but a similar enzyme from a human loses its activity at that temperature. Which is the most likely explanation?
The bacterial enzyme has no tertiary structure.
The human enzyme has a different genetic code.
The bacterial enzyme has more stabilising bonds (such as disulfide bridges and ionic bonds) maintaining its tertiary structure.
The human enzyme lacks peptide bonds at high temperature.

Heat disrupts the weaker bonds that hold tertiary structure, changing the active site (denaturation). Extra stabilising interactions help the bacterial enzyme keep its shape. Peptide bonds are not broken by denaturation, and the genetic code is universal.
bio34a1-psp-6
Describe how a peptide bond is formed between two amino acids. (2 marks)
A condensation reaction occurs between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next; a molecule of water is released and a covalent peptide bond (C–N) forms between them.
bio34a1-psp-7
A single-base substitution in a gene changes one amino acid in an enzyme from a hydrophobic amino acid to a charged amino acid. Explain how this could affect the function of the enzyme. (3 marks)

The change alters the primary structure of the polypeptide; this changes the interactions between R groups (e.g. hydrophobic interactions, ionic bonds) and therefore the way the polypeptide folds into its tertiary structure; if the shape of the active site changes, the substrate may no longer be complementary, so enzyme activity is reduced or lost.
bio34a1-psp-8
Liver cells and skin cells in the same person contain the same genome but have different proteomes. Explain why. (2 marks)

Different genes are switched on (expressed) or off in different cell types due to gene regulation; in addition, alternative splicing and post-translational modification can differ between cells, so each cell type produces a different set of proteins.
vce-bio34-ps-c1
Humans have about 20 000 protein-coding genes but well over 100 000 different proteins. The best explanation is:
Each gene is translated by several different ribosomes
Introns are translated into extra proteins
The genetic code differs between cell types
Alternative splicing of pre-mRNA and post-translational modification
Different combinations of exons can be joined from one gene, and proteins can be modified after translation, so the proteome is larger than the genome.
vce-bio34-protein-secretory-pathway: bio34a1-sec-1
Which sequence correctly shows the path taken by a protein that is secreted from a pancreatic cell?
Free ribosome → Golgi apparatus → rough endoplasmic reticulum → lysosome → plasma membrane
Rough endoplasmic reticulum → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
Nucleus → smooth endoplasmic reticulum → mitochondrion → plasma membrane
Golgi apparatus → rough endoplasmic reticulum → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane

Secreted proteins are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, enter the ER lumen, travel in transport vesicles to the Golgi apparatus for modification and packaging, and leave in secretory vesicles that fuse with the plasma membrane (exocytosis).
bio34a1-sec-2
The main role of the Golgi apparatus in the secretory pathway is to
synthesise polypeptides from mRNA.
produce ATP for exocytosis.
modify, sort and package proteins into vesicles.
transcribe genes coding for secreted proteins.

The Golgi apparatus receives proteins from the rough ER, modifies them (for example by adding carbohydrate groups), sorts them and packages them into vesicles. Polypeptide synthesis happens at ribosomes, and ATP comes mainly from mitochondria.
bio34a1-sec-3
The process by which a secretory vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell is called
exocytosis.
endocytosis.
phagocytosis.
facilitated diffusion.
Exocytosis releases vesicle contents to the outside as the vesicle membrane fuses with the plasma membrane. Endocytosis and phagocytosis bring material into the cell.
bio34a1-sec-4

Researchers add a radioactively labelled amino acid to cultured antibody-secreting plasma cells for 5 minutes, then track the radioactivity. Which order of appearance of the label is expected over the next hour?
Golgi apparatus, then rough ER, then outside the cell
Nucleus, then rough ER, then Golgi apparatus
Mitochondria, then Golgi apparatus, then secretory vesicles
Rough ER, then Golgi apparatus, then secretory vesicles, then outside the cell

The labelled amino acid is built into proteins at ribosomes on the rough ER first, then moves to the Golgi, then into secretory vesicles, and finally outside the cell. Proteins are not made in the nucleus.
bio34a1-sec-5
A cell has a mutation that prevents transport vesicles from budding off the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The most likely consequence is that
the secreted protein accumulates in the rough ER and is not secreted.
the protein is secreted faster because it skips the Golgi.
the protein is translated by free ribosomes instead.
the cell cannot transcribe the gene for the protein.

Without vesicles to carry proteins from the rough ER to the Golgi, the protein builds up in the ER and does not reach the plasma membrane. Transcription in the nucleus is not affected by vesicle transport.
bio34a1-sec-6
Describe the role of the rough endoplasmic reticulum in the production of a protein hormone such as insulin. (2 marks)

Ribosomes attached to the rough ER translate the mRNA, and the growing polypeptide enters the ER lumen; within the ER the polypeptide is folded and may be modified, then packaged into transport vesicles that carry it to the Golgi apparatus.
bio34a1-sec-7

Cells that secrete large amounts of digestive enzymes, such as those in the pancreas, have large amounts of rough ER and many mitochondria. Explain why each feature is useful to these cells. (2 marks)

Extensive rough ER provides many ribosomes and space to synthesise and fold large amounts of protein for secretion; many mitochondria supply ATP needed for protein synthesis and for vesicle transport and exocytosis.
bio34a1-sec-8
Outline the steps involved in the export of a protein from a cell, beginning with transcription of the gene. (3 marks)

The gene is transcribed into mRNA in the nucleus, which is processed and exported to the cytoplasm; the mRNA is translated by ribosomes on the rough ER and the polypeptide enters the ER lumen where it folds, then travels in a transport vesicle to the Golgi apparatus; the Golgi modifies and packages the protein into a secretory vesicle, which moves to and fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing the protein by exocytosis.
vce-bio34-psp-c1
Pancreatic cells are given a radioactive amino acid. In which order would radioactivity appear as an enzyme is made and exported?
Rough ER → transport vesicle → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
Golgi apparatus → rough ER → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane
Nucleus → rough ER → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane
Free ribosome → mitochondrion → Golgi apparatus → plasma membrane
Secreted proteins are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, carried in vesicles to the Golgi to be modified and packaged, then exported by exocytosis.
vce-bio34-enzymes-for-dna-manipulation: bio34a1-edm-1
The restriction enzyme EcoRI recognises the sequence 5′-GAATTC-3′ and cuts between G and A on each strand. The type of ends produced are
blunt ends with no overhanging nucleotides.
sticky ends with single-stranded 5′-AATT overhangs.
sticky ends with single-stranded 3′-GC overhangs.
ends that cannot be joined by DNA ligase.

Cutting G^AATTC on both antiparallel strands leaves staggered cuts with complementary 5′-AATT single-stranded overhangs (sticky ends). Blunt ends occur when both strands are cut at the same position, e.g. SmaI.
bio34a1-edm-2
Which enzyme would a scientist use to produce DNA without introns from the mature mRNA of a human gene?
DNA ligase
Restriction endonuclease
Reverse transcriptase
RNA polymerase

Reverse transcriptase synthesises complementary DNA (cDNA) from an mRNA template. Since mature mRNA has had its introns removed, the cDNA lacks introns, which is useful for expressing human genes in bacteria.
bio34a1-edm-3
The role of DNA ligase in gene cloning is to
cut DNA at specific recognition sites.
separate the two strands of DNA by breaking hydrogen bonds.
copy DNA by adding nucleotides to a primer.
join DNA fragments by forming phosphodiester bonds in the sugar-phosphate backbone.

DNA ligase catalyses formation of phosphodiester bonds between adjacent nucleotides, sealing the backbone of joined fragments. Cutting at recognition sites is done by restriction enzymes; copying is done by DNA polymerase.
bio34a1-edm-4

A linear DNA molecule is cut with a restriction enzyme that has 3 recognition sites in the molecule. A circular plasmid is cut with an enzyme that also has 3 recognition sites. How many fragments are produced from each?
Linear: 4 fragments; circular: 3 fragments
Linear: 3 fragments; circular: 4 fragments
Linear: 3 fragments; circular: 3 fragments
Linear: 4 fragments; circular: 4 fragments
Cutting a linear molecule n times produces n + 1 fragments (4), whereas cutting a circular molecule n times produces n fragments (3), because there are no free ends to begin with.
bio34a1-edm-5
A scientist wants to insert a gene into a plasmid. The gene is flanked by BamHI sites, and the plasmid has one BamHI site. Why should both be cut with BamHI?
BamHI also acts as a ligase to join the fragments.
Using the same enzyme produces complementary sticky ends that can base pair with each other.
BamHI cuts only plasmid DNA, so the gene is not damaged.
BamHI produces blunt ends that are joined more efficiently than sticky ends.

Cutting both with the same restriction enzyme produces complementary sticky ends, so the gene and plasmid ends can base pair by hydrogen bonding before ligase seals the backbone. Restriction enzymes do not join DNA.
bio34a1-edm-6
Distinguish between DNA polymerase and DNA ligase in terms of their function. (2 marks)

DNA polymerase synthesises a new DNA strand by adding free nucleotides one at a time, complementary to a template strand, to the 3′ end of a growing strand/primer; DNA ligase joins two existing DNA fragments together by forming a phosphodiester bond between them, and does not use a template.
bio34a1-edm-7
Explain why restriction enzymes evolved in bacteria and why the bacteria's own DNA is not cut by them. (2 marks)

Restriction enzymes evolved as a defence against bacteriophages, cutting invading viral DNA at specific recognition sites; the bacteria's own DNA is protected because its recognition sites are chemically modified (methylated), so the enzyme cannot cut them.
bio34a1-edm-8

A restriction enzyme recognises a specific six-base-pair sequence. Assuming bases occur randomly and equally, calculate how often, on average, this sequence would be expected to occur in DNA, and explain why an enzyme with a four-base-pair recognition site cuts DNA into smaller fragments. (3 marks)

Probability = (1/4)⁶ = 1/4096, so on average once every 4096 bp; a four-base-pair site has a probability of (1/4)⁴ = 1/256, occurring once every 256 bp on average; it therefore occurs more often, cutting the DNA at more sites and producing more, smaller fragments.
vce-bio34-edm-c1
A gene and a plasmid are both cut with two different restriction enzymes (EcoRI at one end, BamHI at the other). The main advantage is that:
Only one of the two enzymes leaves sticky ends, so the gene can join the plasmid
The gene can only insert in one orientation and the plasmid cannot rejoin itself
Using two enzymes makes the gene shorter, so it fits inside the plasmid
Two different sticky ends mean DNA ligase is not needed to join the fragments
The two different sticky ends are not complementary to each other, which stops self-ligation and forces directional insertion. Ligase is still needed to seal the backbone.
vce-bio34-crispr-cas9: bio34a1-cas-1
In bacteria, the natural role of the CRISPR-Cas system is to
repair DNA damaged by ultraviolet radiation.
regulate the expression of operons.
provide an adaptive defence against bacteriophages by recognising and cutting viral DNA.
transfer plasmids between bacterial cells.

CRISPR-Cas is a bacterial immune system: fragments of phage DNA are stored as spacers in the CRISPR array, and on reinfection the transcribed crRNA guides Cas9 to cut the matching viral DNA. It is not involved in operon regulation or conjugation.
bio34a1-cas-2
In CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, the function of the synthetic guide RNA (sgRNA) is to
cut both strands of the target DNA.
join the cut ends of DNA back together.
act as a template for homology-directed repair.
base pair with a complementary target DNA sequence and direct Cas9 to that site.

The sgRNA contains a spacer sequence (about 20 nucleotides) complementary to the target DNA and binds Cas9, guiding it to the correct location. Cas9 is the endonuclease that cuts DNA; repair is done by the cell.
bio34a1-cas-3
Cas9 from Streptococcus pyogenes will only cut a target sequence if it is located immediately next to a short sequence such as 5′-NGG-3′. This short sequence is called the
protospacer adjacent motif (PAM).
promoter.
operator.
recognition site of EcoRI.
Cas9 must recognise a PAM (5′-NGG-3′ for S. pyogenes Cas9) adjacent to the target before it cuts. This prevents bacteria from cutting the spacers in their own CRISPR array, which lack PAMs.
bio34a1-cas-4
After Cas9 creates a double-stranded break in a gene, the cell repairs it by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). This most often results in
the precise insertion of a new gene supplied by the scientist.
small insertions or deletions that can shift the reading frame and knock out the gene.
removal of all introns from the gene.
duplication of the entire chromosome.

NHEJ joins broken ends without a template and is error-prone, often adding or deleting a few nucleotides. These indels can cause a frameshift and a non-functional protein (a gene knockout). Precise insertion requires homology-directed repair with a template.
bio34a1-cas-5

Researchers want to use CRISPR-Cas9 to disable a gene in a pest species of invasive cane toad. They design an sgRNA, but sequencing shows the target region has no 5′-NGG-3′ sequence nearby. What is the most likely result if they proceed with S. pyogenes Cas9?
Cas9 will cut the DNA at a random location instead.
Cas9 will cut the target but the cell cannot repair it.
The sgRNA will be converted into DNA and inserted into the genome.
Cas9 will not cut the target, even though the sgRNA is complementary, because no PAM is present.

Cas9 requires a PAM adjacent to the target sequence to cut. Without one, no double-stranded break is made at that site. Cas9 does not cut randomly; it is directed by sgRNA complementarity plus the PAM.
bio34a1-cas-6
Describe how a bacterium acquires a 'memory' of a bacteriophage infection using the CRISPR system. (3 marks)

When a bacteriophage injects its DNA, Cas proteins (Cas1 and Cas2) cut out a short segment of the viral DNA; this segment is inserted as a new spacer into the bacterium's CRISPR array between repeat sequences; on a later infection the array is transcribed into crRNA, which guides Cas9 to the matching viral DNA so it is cut and destroyed.
bio34a1-cas-7
Explain how CRISPR-Cas9 can be used to insert a corrected sequence into a gene rather than simply knocking it out. (2 marks)

After Cas9 makes a double-stranded break at the target site, scientists supply a DNA template containing the desired sequence flanked by regions homologous to either side of the break; the cell uses homology-directed repair to copy the template into the break, inserting the corrected sequence.
bio34a1-cas-8
Give one advantage of CRISPR-Cas9 over earlier gene editing methods and one ethical or practical concern about using it to edit human embryos. (2 marks)

Advantage: it is cheaper, faster and more precise/easily targeted, since only the sgRNA sequence needs to be changed to target a new gene; concern: off-target cuts could cause harmful mutations, and edits to embryos are heritable (germline) and passed on to future generations without their consent.
vce-bio34-cr-c1
A gRNA is designed to be perfectly complementary to a 20-nucleotide target, but Cas9 does not cut. The most likely reason is that:
The gRNA is too similar to the target
Cas9 only cuts RNA
There is no PAM sequence next to the target
The target is in an exon
Cas9 needs a short protospacer-adjacent motif (PAM, such as NGG) next to the target sequence before it will cut.
vce-bio34-pcr-and-gel-electrophoresis: bio34a1-pcr-1
Which option correctly matches each step of PCR with its approximate temperature?
Denaturation 72 °C; annealing 95 °C; extension 55 °C
Denaturation 55 °C; annealing 72 °C; extension 95 °C
Denaturation 95 °C; annealing 55 °C; extension 72 °C
Denaturation 37 °C; annealing 55 °C; extension 95 °C
DNA strands separate at about 95 °C, primers anneal at about 50–65 °C (e.g. 55 °C), and Taq polymerase extends the primers at its optimum of about 72 °C.
bio34a1-pcr-2
Taq polymerase is used in PCR rather than human DNA polymerase because Taq polymerase
is stable at the high temperatures used to denature DNA.
does not require primers.
can copy RNA as well as DNA.
joins Okazaki fragments together.
Taq polymerase comes from the thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus, so it does not denature at around 95 °C and is not destroyed in each cycle. It still requires primers.
bio34a1-pcr-3
A forensic scientist starts PCR with 5 copies of a target DNA sequence. Assuming the amount doubles every cycle, how many copies are present after 10 cycles?
Copies = initial × 2ⁿ = 5 × 2¹⁰ = 5 × 1024 = 5120. 1024 is the result from a single starting copy.
bio34a1-pcr-4
In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move towards the positive electrode because
the agarose gel is positively charged.
the phosphate groups in the DNA backbone are negatively charged.
the nitrogenous bases are positively charged.
smaller fragments are attracted more strongly by the anode.
DNA carries a negative charge from its phosphate groups, so it migrates towards the positive electrode (anode). Fragment size affects speed through the gel matrix, not the direction of movement.
bio34a1-pcr-5

A DNA ladder with bands of 100, 300, 500 and 1000 bp is run beside a sample. The sample band travels further than the 300 bp band but not as far as the 100 bp band. The size of the sample fragment is approximately
50 bp
400 bp
200 bp
700 bp
Smaller fragments travel further through the gel. A band between the 300 bp and 100 bp markers is between those sizes, so about 200 bp. 400 bp would lie between the 300 and 500 bp bands.
bio34a1-pcr-6
Explain the role of primers in PCR and why two different primers are needed. (2 marks)

Primers are short single-stranded DNA sequences complementary to the ends of the target region, providing a 3′ end from which DNA polymerase can begin adding nucleotides; two primers are needed because each binds to a different strand (forward and reverse) at opposite ends of the target, so both strands are copied and the region between them is amplified.
bio34a1-pcr-7

DNA profiling can be used to identify a suspect from a blood sample at a crime scene. Explain how PCR and gel electrophoresis are used together to compare short tandem repeats (STRs) from the crime scene and a suspect. (3 marks)

PCR with primers flanking specific STR loci is used to amplify these regions from the small amounts of DNA in each sample; because individuals have different numbers of repeats, the amplified fragments differ in length; the fragments are separated by size using gel electrophoresis and the banding patterns of the crime scene sample and suspect are compared (matching bands at all loci indicate a match).
bio34a1-pcr-8
A student runs a gel but forgets to add a DNA ladder. State why this is a problem and identify one other control that should be included when running PCR products on a gel. (2 marks)

Without a ladder of known fragment sizes, the sizes of the sample fragments cannot be determined (only their relative positions); a negative control (PCR reaction with no template DNA) should also be run to check that reagents are not contaminated with DNA.
vce-bio34-pcr-c1
PCR starts with 3 copies of a target sequence. Assuming perfect doubling, how many copies are there after 10 cycles?
Copies = starting number × 2ⁿ = 3 × 2¹⁰ = 3 × 1024 = 3072.
vce-bio34-recombinant-plasmids-and-trans: bio34a1-rpt-1
Bacterial plasmids are useful as vectors in gene cloning because they
are linear molecules that integrate into the bacterial chromosome.
contain introns that allow eukaryotic genes to be spliced.
are found only in eukaryotic cells.
are small circular DNA molecules that replicate independently and can carry inserted genes.
Plasmids are small, circular, double-stranded DNA molecules with their own origin of replication, so they copy independently of the chromosome and can carry a gene of interest into a host cell.
bio34a1-rpt-2
Which method is commonly used to make bacterial cells take up recombinant plasmids?
Treating cells with calcium chloride and applying a heat shock
Cutting cells with restriction enzymes
Exposing cells to ultraviolet light
Adding reverse transcriptase to the culture

Calcium chloride treatment followed by a brief heat shock (e.g. 42 °C) makes the bacterial membrane more permeable to plasmids. Electroporation is another method. Restriction enzymes cut DNA, not cells.
bio34a1-rpt-3
After transformation, bacteria are spread onto agar containing ampicillin. The plasmid used carries an ampicillin-resistance gene. Bacterial colonies that grow are those that
contain the human gene of interest, regardless of whether they took up a plasmid.
have taken up a plasmid, which may or may not contain the gene of interest.
have not taken up any plasmid.
have produced the human protein.

Only bacteria containing a plasmid (with its ampicillin-resistance gene) survive. Both recombinant and non-recombinant plasmids carry the resistance gene, so a second marker (e.g. lacZ) is needed to identify colonies with the insert.
bio34a1-rpt-4
A plasmid contains the lacZ gene, which contains the restriction site where the gene of interest is inserted. On agar containing X-gal and ampicillin, white colonies indicate bacteria that
did not take up any plasmid.
took up a plasmid without the insert, producing functional β-galactosidase.
took up a recombinant plasmid in which the insert disrupted lacZ.
are resistant to X-gal.

Inserting the gene into lacZ disrupts it, so no functional β-galactosidase is made and X-gal is not broken down into a blue product, leaving white colonies. Blue colonies contain plasmids without the insert. Bacteria with no plasmid do not grow on ampicillin.
bio34a1-rpt-5

Human insulin was first produced in E. coli by inserting the genes for the A and B chains separately, using cDNA or synthetic DNA rather than the human genomic gene. Why was the genomic gene unsuitable?
Bacteria cannot read the human genetic code.
The genomic gene is too small to fit in a plasmid.
Bacteria do not have ribosomes.
The human gene contains introns, and bacteria cannot remove introns from mRNA.

Bacteria lack the spliceosomes needed to remove introns, so a genomic eukaryotic gene would be translated incorrectly. cDNA (from mature mRNA) or synthetic DNA lacks introns. The genetic code is universal, so the codons themselves are not the problem.
bio34a1-rpt-6
Outline the steps used to make a recombinant plasmid containing a human gene. (3 marks)

The gene of interest and the plasmid are cut with the same restriction enzyme to produce complementary sticky ends; the gene and plasmid are mixed so their sticky ends base pair by hydrogen bonding; DNA ligase is added to form phosphodiester bonds, sealing the gene into the plasmid to form a recombinant plasmid.
bio34a1-rpt-7
Explain why only a small proportion of bacteria take up a plasmid during transformation, and how scientists identify those that have. (2 marks)

Transformation is inefficient because plasmids must cross the cell membrane and wall, which only happens in a small fraction of cells even after heat shock or electroporation; a selectable marker such as an antibiotic-resistance gene on the plasmid allows only transformed bacteria to grow on agar containing that antibiotic.
bio34a1-rpt-8
A recombinant plasmid has a gene inserted in the correct position, but no protein is produced by the transformed bacteria. Suggest two possible reasons. (2 marks)

Any two: the gene was inserted in the reverse orientation relative to the promoter, so it is not transcribed correctly; the plasmid lacks a bacterial promoter or ribosome binding site upstream of the gene; the gene contains introns that bacteria cannot remove; the protein is degraded by bacterial proteases or requires post-translational modification the bacteria cannot perform.
vce-bio34-rp-c1
A plasmid carries an ampicillin-resistance gene, and its insertion site lies within the lacZ gene. Bacteria are grown on agar with ampicillin and X-gal. Colonies with the recombinant plasmid are:
Blue, because lacZ is working
Absent, because ampicillin kills them
White, because the inserted gene disrupts lacZ
Blue, because the plasmid has ampicillin resistance
Only transformed bacteria grow on ampicillin. A working lacZ breaks down X-gal to give a blue colour; an insert in lacZ disrupts it, so recombinant colonies are white.
vce-bio34-gmos-and-transgenic-organisms-: bio34a1-gmo-1
Which statement best distinguishes a transgenic organism from other genetically modified organisms?
A transgenic organism contains a gene that has been transferred from a different species.
A transgenic organism has had one of its own genes switched off.
A transgenic organism has been produced by selective breeding.
A transgenic organism is any organism grown in a laboratory.
All transgenic organisms are GMOs, but a GMO is only transgenic if it contains DNA from another species. Switching off an organism's own gene (e.g. with CRISPR) produces a GMO that is not transgenic.
bio34a1-gmo-2
Bt cotton, widely grown in Australia, has been modified to contain a gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis. The benefit of this gene is that the plant
is tolerant to the herbicide glyphosate.
produces a protein that is toxic to certain caterpillar pests, reducing the need for insecticide sprays.
fixes its own atmospheric nitrogen.
produces β-carotene in its fibres.

The Bt gene codes for a Cry protein that is toxic to particular insect larvae such as the cotton bollworm, so growers spray less insecticide. Glyphosate tolerance is a different trait found in herbicide-tolerant crops such as some canola.
bio34a1-gmo-3
Golden Rice was engineered to address vitamin A deficiency. The rice contains genes that allow the endosperm to
produce insulin.
resist the herbicide glyphosate.
synthesise β-carotene, a precursor of vitamin A.
grow in saline soil.

Genes from daffodil (or maize) and a soil bacterium were inserted so that rice endosperm produces β-carotene, which the body converts to vitamin A. Herbicide resistance and salt tolerance are different traits.
bio34a1-gmo-4
Agrobacterium tumefaciens is used to produce transgenic plants because it
naturally destroys plant viruses.
is resistant to all antibiotics.
reproduces only inside plant seeds.
naturally transfers a section of DNA from its Ti plasmid into the plant cell's genome.
Agrobacterium transfers T-DNA from its Ti plasmid into plant chromosomes. Scientists replace tumour-causing genes in the T-DNA with the gene of interest so it is integrated into the plant genome.
bio34a1-gmo-5

A farmer has grown glyphosate-tolerant canola and sprayed glyphosate on the same paddock every year for ten years. Glyphosate is now much less effective at controlling ryegrass weeds in that paddock. The best explanation is that
repeated spraying selected for ryegrass plants that carried variations giving glyphosate resistance, which survived and reproduced.
the transgene moved from the canola to every ryegrass plant.
the ryegrass deliberately changed its genes in response to the herbicide.
glyphosate breaks down faster in older soil.

Glyphosate acts as a selection pressure: resistant ryegrass individuals survive and reproduce, so resistance increases in the population over time. Organisms do not change their genes deliberately, and gene flow to every weed plant is very unlikely.
bio34a1-gmo-6
Describe how a transgenic plant could be produced using Agrobacterium tumefaciens. (3 marks)

The gene of interest (with a marker gene) is inserted into the T-DNA region of a Ti plasmid, replacing the tumour-causing genes, using restriction enzymes and ligase; the recombinant plasmid is put into Agrobacterium, which is used to infect plant cells or tissue, transferring the T-DNA into the plant genome; transformed cells are selected (e.g. on antibiotic or herbicide media) and grown by tissue culture into whole plants that carry the gene.
bio34a1-gmo-7
Discuss one biological benefit and one biological risk of growing Bt crops in Australia. (2 marks)

Benefit: reduced use of broad-spectrum insecticide sprays, protecting non-target insects and reducing costs while increasing yield; risk: target pests may evolve resistance to the Bt toxin through natural selection (managed using refuge crops), or the transgene may spread to related wild plants by cross-pollination.
bio34a1-gmo-8
Some people argue that genetically modified crops are essential for food security, while others oppose them. Give one social or economic argument for and one against the use of GM crops. (2 marks)

For: GM crops can increase yields, resist pests or drought, or improve nutrition (e.g. Golden Rice), helping feed growing populations; against: patented GM seed may need to be bought each season, increasing costs and dependence of farmers on a few large companies, and some consumers and export markets reject GM products.
vce-bio34-gmo-c1
Which statement about genetically modified and transgenic organisms is correct?
Every transgenic organism is a GMO, but not every GMO is transgenic
Every GMO contains DNA from another species
Transgenic organisms have had a gene deleted using CRISPR
GMOs and transgenic organisms are identical terms
A GMO has had its genome altered in any way (including editing its own genes); a transgenic organism contains DNA from a different species.
vce-bio34-enzymes-and-coenzymes: bio34a2-enz-1
Which statement best describes the induced fit model of enzyme action?
The active site is a rigid shape that exactly matches the substrate before binding
The enzyme is permanently altered once it has catalysed a reaction
The substrate changes the primary structure of the enzyme so that it can bind
The active site changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, forming a tighter enzyme–substrate complex

In the induced fit model the active site is complementary but flexible, moulding around the substrate as it binds. The rigid, exact-match idea describes the older lock-and-key model, and enzymes are not consumed or permanently changed.
bio34a2-enz-2
Enzymes increase the rate of a biochemical reaction by
lowering the activation energy of the reaction
supplying energy to the reactants
increasing the activation energy of the reaction
shifting the equilibrium so that more product forms

Enzymes are biological catalysts that provide an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy. They do not supply energy and do not change the final position of equilibrium; they only speed up attainment of it.
bio34a2-enz-3
Which coenzyme is correctly matched to its loaded form and the pathway in which the loaded form is produced?
ADP → ATP, produced only in the Calvin cycle
NAD⁺ → NADH, produced in the light-independent stage of photosynthesis
NADP⁺ → NADPH, produced in the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis
NADPH → NADP⁺, produced in glycolysis

NADP⁺ accepts electrons and a proton to become NADPH in the light-dependent stage, and NADPH is unloaded in the Calvin cycle. NADH is made in cellular respiration, not the light-independent stage, and the Calvin cycle uses ATP rather than producing it.
bio34a2-enz-4
A student describes a coenzyme as 'a protein that binds permanently to an enzyme's active site'. The best correction is that a coenzyme is
an inorganic ion that changes the shape of the substrate
a non-protein organic molecule that assists an enzyme, often by carrying electrons, protons or chemical groups between reactions
the product of an enzyme-catalysed reaction that inhibits further activity
a second enzyme that works on the same substrate

Coenzymes are organic, non-protein molecules (e.g. NAD⁺, NADP⁺, FAD, ATP/ADP) that bind temporarily and shuttle electrons, protons or phosphate groups between reactions. Inorganic helpers such as Mg²⁺ are cofactors but not coenzymes.
bio34a2-enz-5
In a metabolic pathway A → B → C → D, each step is catalysed by a different enzyme (E1, E2, E3). A mutation results in a non-functional E2. Which molecule would be expected to accumulate in the cell?
A
C
D
B
E2 converts B into C. Without functional E2, B cannot be converted, so B builds up while C and D are depleted. A still converts to B because E1 is functional.
bio34a2-enz-6
Explain why each enzyme usually catalyses only one specific reaction. Refer to protein structure in your answer. (3 marks)

Enzymes are proteins whose tertiary structure is determined by the sequence of amino acids (primary structure); folding produces an active site with a specific three-dimensional shape and chemical properties (charge, hydrophobicity); only a substrate with a complementary shape and chemistry can bind to the active site to form an enzyme–substrate complex, so each enzyme is specific to one substrate/reaction.
bio34a2-enz-7
ATP is often described as the 'energy currency' of the cell. Describe how the ATP/ADP cycle couples energy-releasing and energy-requiring reactions in a cell. (3 marks)

Energy released from catabolic reactions such as cellular respiration is used to add an inorganic phosphate (Pi) to ADP, forming ATP; ATP diffuses to sites where energy is needed; hydrolysis of ATP to ADP + Pi releases energy that drives anabolic or energy-requiring processes such as active transport, muscle contraction or protein synthesis; ADP + Pi are then recycled back to respiration to be reloaded.
bio34a2-enz-8
Distinguish between the roles of loaded and unloaded coenzymes, using NADH and NAD⁺ in cellular respiration as an example. (2 marks)

Unloaded coenzymes (NAD⁺) accept electrons and hydrogen ions released during glycolysis and the Krebs cycle, becoming loaded (NADH); loaded NADH carries these electrons and protons to the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane, where it is unloaded (returning to NAD⁺) and the energy is used to produce ATP.
vce-bio34-ec-c1
Which statement about NADP in photosynthesis is correct?
NADPH is loaded in the stroma during the Calvin cycle and unloaded in the thylakoid membranes
NADP⁺ accepts electrons and H⁺ in the light-dependent stage; NADPH donates them in the Calvin cycle
NADP⁺ is an enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide to RuBP in the Calvin cycle in the stroma
NADPH is unloaded in the light-dependent stage to provide the electrons for splitting water
Coenzymes cycle between loaded and unloaded forms, carrying electrons and protons from one stage to the next.
vce-bio34-factors-affecting-enzymes-and-: bio34a2-inh-1
A drug binds to a site on an enzyme other than the active site, changing the shape of the active site so the substrate can no longer bind. This drug is acting as a
competitive inhibitor
coenzyme
non-competitive inhibitor
substrate analogue

Binding at a site other than the active site (an allosteric site) and altering active site shape is non-competitive inhibition. Competitive inhibitors and substrate analogues bind the active site itself.
bio34a2-inh-2

An enzyme from a hot-spring bacterium has an optimum temperature of 75 °C. When the enzyme is incubated at 95 °C for 30 minutes and then cooled to 75 °C, it shows almost no activity. The most likely explanation is that at 95 °C
the enzyme was denatured, permanently changing the shape of its active site
the substrate molecules moved too quickly to bind
the enzyme's primary structure was broken into individual amino acids
the enzyme became inactive temporarily and needs more time to recover

High temperatures break the hydrogen bonds and other interactions holding the tertiary structure, denaturing the enzyme. The change is irreversible here, so cooling does not restore activity. Peptide bonds (primary structure) are not broken by denaturation.
bio34a2-inh-3

In an experiment, the rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction increases as substrate concentration increases, then plateaus. Adding more enzyme raises the plateau. What limited the reaction rate at the plateau before extra enzyme was added?
Substrate concentration
Temperature
pH of the solution
Enzyme concentration (all active sites were occupied)

At the plateau all active sites are saturated, so adding substrate has no effect; the rate is limited by the number of enzyme molecules. Adding more enzyme provides more active sites and raises the maximum rate, confirming enzyme concentration was limiting.
bio34a2-inh-4
The effect of a competitive inhibitor on an enzyme can be reduced by
decreasing the concentration of substrate
increasing the concentration of substrate
lowering the temperature to 4 °C
adding a non-competitive inhibitor

Competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate for the active site. Raising substrate concentration increases the likelihood that substrate, rather than inhibitor, occupies the active site. This does not overcome non-competitive inhibition.
bio34a2-inh-5
Pepsin works in the stomach at about pH 2, while trypsin works in the small intestine at about pH 8. If pepsin is moved into a solution at pH 8, its activity drops sharply because
pepsin is digested by the alkaline solution
pepsin requires trypsin as a coenzyme at pH 8
the change in pH alters the charges on amino acid R groups, disrupting the bonds that maintain the active site shape
the substrate denatures at pH 8 but the enzyme is unaffected

Changes in pH alter the ionisation of R groups, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the tertiary structure, so the active site loses its complementary shape. Each enzyme has an optimum pH matched to its environment.
bio34a2-inh-6

Some pesticides act as irreversible inhibitors of acetylcholinesterase, an enzyme needed for normal nerve function in insects. Explain how an irreversible inhibitor differs from a reversible inhibitor and why irreversible inhibition is effective as a pesticide. (3 marks)

An irreversible inhibitor forms strong (often covalent) bonds with the enzyme, permanently inactivating it; a reversible inhibitor binds with weak bonds and can detach, so enzyme activity can be restored; because the insect's acetylcholinesterase is permanently inactivated, enzyme activity cannot recover (new enzyme must be synthesised), so nerve function fails and the insect dies.
bio34a2-inh-7

A student measured the activity of catalase (which breaks down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen) from potato at 10 °C, 25 °C, 37 °C and 60 °C by measuring the volume of oxygen produced in 2 minutes. Activity was highest at 37 °C and almost zero at 60 °C. Explain the results at 10 °C and at 60 °C. (3 marks)

At 10 °C the enzyme and substrate molecules have low kinetic energy, so there are fewer successful collisions between substrate and active site and fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form per unit time, giving low activity; the enzyme is not denatured at 10 °C, so activity would increase if warmed; at 60 °C heat disrupts the hydrogen bonds maintaining tertiary structure, so the enzyme denatures, the active site loses its shape and substrate can no longer bind, so activity is near zero.
bio34a2-inh-8
Many metabolic pathways are regulated by end-product inhibition. Describe how this works and explain one benefit to the cell. (2 marks)

The final product of a pathway binds to (often allosterically inhibits) an enzyme early in the pathway, reducing its activity when product levels are high; this prevents over-production of the product and avoids wasting substrate and energy, with the pathway resuming when product levels fall.
vce-bio34-fe-c1
Adding much more substrate restores the maximum reaction rate when an inhibitor is present. The inhibitor is most likely:
Non-competitive, binding to an allosteric site
Irreversible, binding permanently to the active site
A coenzyme
Competitive, binding to the active site
Extra substrate out-competes a competitive inhibitor for the active site. A non-competitive inhibitor changes the active site's shape, so more substrate cannot help.
vce-bio34-photosynthesis: bio34a2-ps-1
The light-dependent stage of photosynthesis occurs in the
thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast
stroma of the chloroplast
inner membrane of the mitochondrion
cytosol of the mesophyll cell

Chlorophyll and the electron transport proteins of the light-dependent stage are embedded in the thylakoid membranes (stacked into grana). The stroma is the site of the light-independent stage (Calvin cycle).
bio34a2-ps-2
Which row correctly shows the inputs and outputs of the light-independent stage (Calvin cycle)?
Inputs: H₂O, NADP⁺, ADP + Pi. Outputs: O₂, NADPH, ATP
Inputs: CO₂, H₂O, light. Outputs: O₂, NADPH
Inputs: glucose, O₂. Outputs: CO₂, H₂O, ATP
Inputs: CO₂, NADPH, ATP. Outputs: glucose, NADP⁺, ADP + Pi

The Calvin cycle fixes CO₂ using energy from ATP and electrons/protons from NADPH, producing glucose and returning NADP⁺ and ADP + Pi to the light-dependent stage. The option with H₂O, NADP⁺ and ADP + Pi as inputs describes the light-dependent stage.
bio34a2-ps-3
A scientist supplies a plant with water containing the oxygen isotope ¹⁸O. In which product of photosynthesis would the ¹⁸O first be detected?
Glucose
NADPH
Carbon dioxide
Oxygen gas released from the leaf
In the light-dependent stage, water is split (photolysis) to provide electrons and H⁺; the oxygen atoms from water are released as O₂. The oxygen atoms in glucose come from CO₂.
bio34a2-ps-4
A plant is moved from bright light into darkness. In the first few minutes, the rate of the Calvin cycle falls mainly because
the supply of ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent stage stops
CO₂ can no longer diffuse into the leaf
rubisco is denatured in the dark
glucose accumulates and inhibits rubisco

The Calvin cycle does not use light directly, but it depends on ATP and NADPH from the light-dependent stage. In darkness these are no longer produced, so the light-independent reactions slow and stop once existing supplies are used.
bio34a2-ps-5

A graph shows the rate of photosynthesis of a wheat plant increasing with light intensity until it plateaus at a high light intensity. Raising CO₂ concentration at this high light intensity causes the rate to increase further. What was the limiting factor at the plateau?
Light intensity
Water availability
CO₂ concentration
Chlorophyll concentration
At the plateau, increasing light has no effect, so light is not limiting. Because adding CO₂ increased the rate, CO₂ concentration was the factor limiting the Calvin cycle at that point.
bio34a2-ps-6
Describe the role of rubisco in photosynthesis and explain why its activity is affected by temperature. (3 marks)

Rubisco is the enzyme in the stroma that catalyses carbon fixation, combining CO₂ with a 5-carbon compound (RuBP) at the start of the Calvin cycle; like other enzymes it has an optimum temperature; below the optimum, fewer successful collisions occur so the rate is slower, and above the optimum the enzyme begins to denature (and binds O₂ more readily), reducing the rate of carbon fixation.
bio34a2-ps-7
Write a balanced overall equation for photosynthesis in plants, and name where in the chloroplast each of the reactants is used. (3 marks)

6CO₂ + 12H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ + 6H₂O (in the presence of light and chlorophyll; 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ also accepted); water is split in the light-dependent stage in the thylakoid membranes (grana); carbon dioxide is fixed in the light-independent stage (Calvin cycle) in the stroma.
bio34a2-ps-8
Explain why the light-dependent and light-independent stages of photosynthesis are described as interdependent. (2 marks)

The light-dependent stage produces ATP and NADPH, which are required to power and reduce CO₂ in the light-independent stage; the light-independent stage regenerates ADP + Pi and NADP⁺, which must return to the thylakoids for the light-dependent stage to continue, so neither stage can continue for long without the other.
vce-bio34-ph-c1
A plant is given water labelled with the oxygen isotope ¹⁸O. The label first appears in:
Glucose
Carbon dioxide
ATP
Oxygen gas released by the plant
Water is split in the light-dependent stage, and its oxygen atoms are released as O₂. The oxygen in glucose comes from CO₂.
vce-bio34-c3-c4-and-cam-plants: bio34a2-c4-1
Photorespiration in C3 plants occurs when
chlorophyll absorbs too much light and is damaged
rubisco binds oxygen instead of carbon dioxide, reducing the efficiency of carbon fixation
the plant respires faster than it photosynthesises at night
PEP carboxylase binds oxygen in the bundle sheath cells

Rubisco can bind O₂ as well as CO₂. When O₂ binds, energy and fixed carbon are wasted and CO₂ is released, lowering photosynthetic efficiency. PEP carboxylase does not bind O₂, which is why C4 plants use it.
bio34a2-c4-2
C4 plants such as maize and kangaroo grass reduce photorespiration by
opening their stomata only at night
storing CO₂ as malic acid in vacuoles during the day
producing a form of rubisco that cannot bind oxygen
spatially separating initial CO₂ fixation in mesophyll cells from the Calvin cycle in bundle sheath cells

In C4 plants PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into a 4-carbon compound in mesophyll cells; this is moved to bundle sheath cells, where CO₂ is released at high concentration around rubisco. Separating stages in time (night/day) describes CAM plants.
bio34a2-c4-3
A pineapple plant has its stomata open at night and closed during the day. Which statement correctly describes carbon fixation in this plant?
CO₂ is fixed by rubisco at night and stored as glucose
CO₂ diffuses directly to rubisco during the day because the stomata are closed
CO₂ is fixed into a 4-carbon acid at night and released to rubisco for the Calvin cycle during the day
The Calvin cycle runs only at night when the stomata are open

Pineapple is a CAM plant. At night, PEP carboxylase fixes CO₂ into organic acids (malate) stored in vacuoles. During the day, with stomata closed, CO₂ is released internally and enters the Calvin cycle, which needs ATP and NADPH from light.
bio34a2-c4-4
In which environment would a CAM plant be expected to have the greatest advantage over a C3 plant?
A hot, arid desert with very low water availability
A cool, shaded rainforest floor
A temperate pasture with regular rainfall
A freshwater pond

CAM plants keep stomata closed during the hot day, greatly reducing water loss while still fixing carbon. This trade-off is most beneficial in hot, dry environments. In cool, moist conditions C3 plants are generally more efficient.
bio34a2-c4-5

Researchers grew a C3 plant and a C4 plant at 35 °C under bright light. The C4 plant had a much higher rate of photosynthesis. Under cool conditions (15 °C) the C3 plant performed slightly better. The best explanation for the result at 15 °C is that
C4 plants cannot photosynthesise below 20 °C
rubisco is denatured at 15 °C in C4 plants
C3 plants have more chloroplasts at low temperatures
at lower temperatures photorespiration in C3 plants is low, so the extra ATP cost of the C4 pathway is not offset
Concentrating CO₂ in C4 plants costs extra ATP. When it is cool, rubisco binds O₂ less often and stomata can stay open, so C3 plants lose little to photorespiration and avoid this energy cost.
bio34a2-c4-6
Explain why hot, dry conditions increase the rate of photorespiration in C3 plants. (3 marks)

In hot, dry conditions C3 plants close their stomata to reduce water loss by transpiration; this prevents CO₂ from diffusing into the leaf while O₂ produced by the light-dependent stage builds up, so the ratio of O₂ to CO₂ around rubisco increases; rubisco therefore binds O₂ more often (and its affinity for O₂ relative to CO₂ increases at higher temperatures), increasing photorespiration and reducing glucose production.
bio34a2-c4-7
Compare C4 and CAM plants by describing one similarity and one difference in how they minimise photorespiration. (2 marks)

Similarity: both first fix CO₂ using PEP carboxylase (which does not bind O₂) into a 4-carbon compound, later releasing CO₂ to rubisco for the Calvin cycle; difference: C4 plants separate the two steps spatially (mesophyll and bundle sheath cells) during the day, whereas CAM plants separate them in time (CO₂ fixed at night, Calvin cycle during the day) within the same cell.
bio34a2-c4-8
A farmer in northern Australia is choosing between a C3 crop and a C4 crop for a hot, sunny region with limited irrigation. Recommend a crop type and justify your choice. (3 marks)

Recommend the C4 crop; in hot, sunny, dry conditions stomata may partially close, and a C3 crop would suffer high photorespiration, reducing yield; the C4 crop concentrates CO₂ around rubisco in bundle sheath cells, so photorespiration is minimised and it can photosynthesise efficiently with stomata only partly open, giving higher yield and better water use efficiency.
vce-bio34-c4-c1
How do C4 and CAM plants reduce photorespiration?
C4 plants separate initial CO₂ fixation and the Calvin cycle in space; CAM plants separate them in time
C4 plants separate initial CO₂ fixation and the Calvin cycle in time; CAM plants separate them in space
Both replace rubisco with an enzyme that cannot bind oxygen, so the Calvin cycle runs without it
Both open their stomata only at midday, when the CO₂ concentration inside the leaf is highest
C4: CO₂ is fixed in mesophyll cells and released to rubisco in bundle-sheath cells. CAM: CO₂ is fixed at night (stomata open) and used in the Calvin cycle by day.
vce-bio34-cellular-respiration: bio34a2-cr-1
Glycolysis occurs in the
mitochondrial matrix
cytosol
inner mitochondrial membrane
stroma
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol and does not need oxygen. The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix and the electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae).
bio34a2-cr-2
Which of the following is the net yield of glycolysis per molecule of glucose?
6 CO₂, 2 ATP and 6 NADH
2 pyruvate, 4 ATP and 2 FADH₂
2 pyruvate, 2 ATP and 2 NADH
2 lactate, 2 ATP and 2 NAD⁺
Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate, producing a net 2 ATP (4 made, 2 used) and 2 NADH. CO₂ is released in the link reaction and Krebs cycle, not glycolysis.
bio34a2-cr-3
Oxygen is required in aerobic cellular respiration because it
is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain, combining with electrons and H⁺ to form water
is used to split glucose in glycolysis
combines with carbon to form CO₂ in the Krebs cycle
is a coenzyme that carries electrons from the Krebs cycle

At the end of the electron transport chain, O₂ accepts electrons and H⁺ to form H₂O. Without O₂ the chain stops, NADH cannot be unloaded and most ATP production ceases. The CO₂ released in the Krebs cycle comes from the carbon skeletons of the fuel molecules.
bio34a2-cr-4
A poison blocks the electron transport chain in mitochondria. Which of the following would occur first in an affected cell?
The concentration of NAD⁺ in the mitochondrial matrix would increase
The cell would produce more CO₂
Glycolysis would stop immediately because it requires oxygen
The concentration of NADH would increase and ATP production would fall sharply

If the chain is blocked, NADH and FADH₂ cannot be unloaded, so NADH accumulates and NAD⁺ is depleted. The electron transport chain produces most ATP, so ATP levels fall sharply. Glycolysis does not need oxygen directly.
bio34a2-cr-5
Which stage of aerobic cellular respiration produces the most ATP per glucose molecule, and where does it occur?
Glycolysis, in the cytosol
Krebs cycle, in the mitochondrial matrix
Krebs cycle, on the outer mitochondrial membrane
Electron transport chain, on the inner mitochondrial membrane (cristae)

Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle each produce only 2 ATP per glucose. The electron transport chain on the cristae uses energy from loaded coenzymes to produce the large majority of ATP (approximately 26–34 ATP).
bio34a2-cr-6
Outline the Krebs cycle by stating its location, inputs and outputs per glucose molecule. (3 marks)

Location: mitochondrial matrix; inputs: acetyl CoA (derived from 2 pyruvate), NAD⁺, FAD, ADP + Pi; outputs: CO₂ (released as waste), 2 ATP, loaded coenzymes NADH and FADH₂ (which carry electrons and H⁺ to the electron transport chain).
bio34a2-cr-7
Muscle cells of an athlete in training have more mitochondria than those of an untrained person. Explain how this structural difference benefits the athlete during sustained exercise. (2 marks)

More mitochondria means more sites for the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain (more cristae surface area), so the rate of aerobic respiration increases; more ATP can be produced aerobically to supply energy for muscle contraction during sustained exercise, reducing reliance on anaerobic respiration and lactate build-up.
bio34a2-cr-8
Explain why the folding of the inner mitochondrial membrane into cristae increases the cell's capacity to produce ATP. (2 marks)

The electron transport chain proteins and ATP synthase are embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane; folding into cristae greatly increases the surface area of this membrane, so more electron transport chains and ATP synthase enzymes are present and more ATP can be produced per mitochondrion.
vce-bio34-cr2-c1
Cyanide blocks the electron transport chain. Which other stage of aerobic respiration stops soon after?
Glycolysis only, because it happens in the cytosol
No other stage, because they are independent
Photosynthesis
The Krebs cycle, because NAD⁺ and FAD are no longer regenerated
The ETC unloads NADH and FADH₂. Without it, NAD⁺ and FAD run out and the Krebs cycle stops. Glycolysis can continue through fermentation.
vce-bio34-anaerobic-respiration-and-ferm: bio34a2-an-1
During intense sprinting, human muscle cells carry out anaerobic respiration. The products of this pathway are
lactate (lactic acid) and 2 ATP
ethanol, CO₂ and 2 ATP
CO₂, H₂O and about 30 ATP
pyruvate, O₂ and 2 ATP

Anaerobic respiration in animals converts glucose to lactate, with a net yield of 2 ATP from glycolysis. Ethanol and CO₂ are the products in yeast (alcoholic fermentation). No CO₂ is produced in lactic acid fermentation.
bio34a2-an-2
The main purpose of converting pyruvate to lactate or ethanol during anaerobic respiration is to
produce additional ATP after glycolysis
release CO₂ for photosynthesis
regenerate NAD⁺ so that glycolysis can continue
remove oxygen from the cell
Glycolysis requires NAD⁺. Without oxygen the electron transport chain cannot unload NADH, so pyruvate is reduced to lactate or ethanol, unloading NADH back to NAD⁺. No extra ATP is made in this step.
bio34a2-an-3
Anaerobic respiration in yeast occurs in the
mitochondrial matrix
cytosol
cristae
nucleus
Both glycolysis and the fermentation step that produces ethanol and CO₂ occur in the cytosol. Mitochondria are not used because the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain depend on oxygen.
bio34a2-an-4

Yeast is placed in a sealed flask containing glucose solution. A CO₂ sensor shows CO₂ being produced throughout the experiment, while an O₂ sensor shows O₂ falling to zero after 20 minutes. After 20 minutes, the yeast is
no longer respiring
producing O₂ by photosynthesis
respiring anaerobically, producing lactate
respiring anaerobically, producing ethanol and CO₂
Once O₂ is used up, yeast switches to anaerobic respiration (alcoholic fermentation), which still releases CO₂ along with ethanol. Lactate is produced by animal cells and some bacteria, not yeast.
bio34a2-an-5
Compared with aerobic respiration, anaerobic respiration of one glucose molecule
produces the same amount of ATP but more CO₂
produces more ATP but more slowly
produces much less ATP because glucose is only partially broken down
requires mitochondria to produce ATP

Anaerobic respiration yields only 2 ATP per glucose because much of the chemical energy remains in lactate or ethanol. Aerobic respiration fully oxidises glucose to CO₂ and H₂O, producing far more ATP.
bio34a2-an-6

Bioethanol can be produced by fermenting plant material such as sugarcane. Describe the biological process by which yeast produces ethanol and identify one advantage of bioethanol as a fuel. (3 marks)

Yeast breaks down glucose by glycolysis in the cytosol into 2 pyruvate, producing 2 ATP and 2 NADH; in the absence of oxygen pyruvate is converted into ethanol and CO₂, which regenerates NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue; advantage: it is a renewable fuel, and the CO₂ released when it burns was recently absorbed by the crop during photosynthesis, so net CO₂ emissions can be lower than for fossil fuels.
bio34a2-an-7
Explain why a sprinter cannot rely on anaerobic respiration for an extended period of time. (2 marks)

Anaerobic respiration produces only 2 ATP per glucose, which cannot meet a high energy demand for long and rapidly uses up glucose; lactate (and associated H⁺) builds up in the muscle, lowering pH, which affects enzyme function and contributes to fatigue, so oxygen is needed to recover.
bio34a2-an-8
A baker notices bread dough rises faster at 30 °C than at 15 °C. Explain this observation. (2 marks)

Dough rises due to CO₂ released by yeast respiration (including fermentation); at 30 °C, closer to the optimum temperature of yeast enzymes, molecules have more kinetic energy and enzyme–substrate collisions are more frequent, so the rate of respiration and CO₂ production is faster than at 15 °C.
vce-bio34-an-c1
Explain why muscle cells short of oxygen convert pyruvate to lactate instead of simply stopping after glycolysis.
Converting pyruvate to lactate regenerates NAD⁺ from NADH. Glycolysis needs NAD⁺, so it can continue and keep producing 2 ATP per glucose.
Without NAD⁺ regeneration glycolysis would stop; the lactate step itself makes no ATP.
vce-bio34-biotechnology-to-improve-yield: bio34a2-bt-1
Scientists aim to use CRISPR-Cas9 to edit the gene for a subunit of rubisco in a C3 crop. Which outcome would most directly improve crop yield?
Rubisco with a reduced tendency to bind O₂ relative to CO₂
Rubisco with an increased affinity for O₂
Rubisco that is active only at night
Rubisco that can no longer bind CO₂
Reducing rubisco's tendency to bind O₂ would lower photorespiration, so more carbon is fixed into glucose, increasing growth and yield. Increased O₂ binding would worsen photorespiration.
bio34a2-bt-2
In CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing, the role of the guide RNA (sgRNA) is to
cut both strands of the DNA
join DNA fragments together
act as the template for DNA repair
direct Cas9 to a specific target DNA sequence by complementary base pairing
The guide RNA has a sequence complementary to the target DNA, directing Cas9 to the correct site. Cas9 is the endonuclease that makes the double-stranded cut, adjacent to a PAM sequence.
bio34a2-bt-3
Which of the following describes an approach to improve the yield of a C3 crop such as rice?
Removing all chlorophyll genes to reduce light absorption
Inserting genes for the C4 pathway enzymes and bundle sheath anatomy so CO₂ is concentrated around rubisco
Inserting genes that keep stomata permanently closed
Knocking out the gene for rubisco
