Research projects aim to engineer C4-like features into rice so CO₂ is concentrated around rubisco, reducing photorespiration and increasing photosynthetic efficiency. The other options would reduce photosynthesis.
bio34a2-bt-4
Second-generation biofuels are made from non-food plant material such as crop stems and woodchips. A key advantage of this approach over first-generation bioethanol made from corn grain is that it
releases no CO₂ when burned
does not require any enzymes
does not compete directly with food production for crops
produces petrol rather than ethanol

Using agricultural waste and non-food biomass avoids diverting food crops (and the land they need) to fuel production. All bioethanol releases CO₂ when burned, and breaking down cellulose requires enzymes (cellulases) before fermentation.
bio34a2-bt-5
Before yeast can ferment cellulose-rich plant waste into ethanol, the cellulose must first be broken down. This is necessary because
yeast can only ferment simple sugars such as glucose, and cellulose is a polysaccharide
cellulose is toxic to yeast
cellulose contains no carbon
yeast respires only aerobically
Cellulose is a polymer of glucose. Yeast lacks cellulases, so enzymes (or other pretreatments) must hydrolyse cellulose into glucose that yeast can take up and ferment to ethanol and CO₂.
bio34a2-bt-6
Describe how CRISPR-Cas9 could be used to knock out a gene in a crop plant, and suggest one way this could improve yield. (3 marks)

A guide RNA complementary to the target gene is designed and delivered with Cas9 into plant cells; Cas9 is guided to the target sequence (next to a PAM) and makes a double-stranded cut; the cell repairs the break by non-homologous end joining, often introducing insertions/deletions that disable the gene; e.g. knocking out a gene that makes the plant susceptible to a disease, or a gene that limits grain size/number, could increase yield.
bio34a2-bt-7

Scientists are investigating ways to increase the efficiency of photosynthesis in crops to feed a growing population. Identify one factor that limits photosynthesis in C3 crops and explain how a biotechnological approach could address it. (3 marks)

Factor: photorespiration / the inefficiency of rubisco, which binds O₂ as well as CO₂; approach: gene editing (e.g. CRISPR-Cas9) or genetic modification to produce a rubisco with greater specificity for CO₂, or insert a CO₂-concentrating mechanism (e.g. C4 pathway genes); this would increase the rate of carbon fixation in the Calvin cycle, producing more glucose for growth and increasing yield.
bio34a2-bt-8
Evaluate the use of sugarcane-based bioethanol as an alternative to petrol in Australia, giving one advantage and one disadvantage. (2 marks)

Advantage: it is renewable and the CO₂ released was recently absorbed during photosynthesis, so it can reduce net greenhouse gas emissions compared with fossil fuels; disadvantage: growing sugarcane for fuel uses land, water and fertiliser that could be used for food production, and processing requires energy inputs that reduce the net benefit.
vce-bio34-by-c1
Scientists are trying to engineer C4 traits into rice (a C3 plant). The main expected benefit in hot, dry conditions is:
Faster cellular respiration, so more ATP is available for growth
Rice could photosynthesise at night, without needing any light
Less photorespiration, so more carbon is fixed per unit of water lost
Rubisco would no longer be needed in the Calvin cycle at all
In heat, C3 plants close their stomata and rubisco binds O₂ more often. A C4 pathway concentrates CO₂ around rubisco.
vce-bio34-pathogens-and-physical-and-che: bio34a2-pb-1
Which of the following is a non-cellular pathogen?
Plasmodium falciparum (a protozoan)
Staphylococcus aureus (a bacterium)
Candida albicans (a fungus)
A prion
Prions are misfolded proteins and viruses are also non-cellular. Bacteria, fungi and protozoa are cellular pathogens.
bio34a2-pb-2
Lysozyme is found in tears and saliva. It is classified as a
physical barrier that traps pathogens
component of the adaptive immune response
microbiological barrier that outcompetes pathogens
chemical barrier that breaks down bacterial cell walls

Lysozyme is an enzyme that hydrolyses peptidoglycan in bacterial cell walls, making it a chemical barrier in the first line of defence. Physical barriers include skin and mucus; microbiological barriers are normal flora.
bio34a2-pb-3
A patient takes a long course of broad-spectrum antibiotics and then develops a fungal infection in the mouth. The most likely explanation is that the antibiotics
killed many of the normal bacterial flora that usually outcompete fungi
stimulated fungal growth directly
destroyed the mucous membranes of the mouth
acted as an antigen that triggered an allergic reaction
Normal flora act as a microbiological barrier by competing for space and nutrients. Antibiotics kill bacteria but not fungi, so removing the normal flora allows fungi such as Candida to overgrow.
bio34a2-pb-4
Which of the following is a physical barrier in plants against pathogen entry?
Production of chitinase enzymes
Production of antimicrobial saponins
A waxy cuticle on the leaf surface
Release of hydrogen peroxide at the infection site
The waxy cuticle physically blocks pathogens and prevents water films that help fungal spores germinate. Saponins, chitinases and hydrogen peroxide are chemical defences.
bio34a2-pb-5
Cells lining the human trachea have cilia and secrete mucus. Smoking damages the cilia. Which effect would be expected in a smoker?
Increased stomach acid production
Pathogens trapped in mucus are less effectively moved out of the airways, increasing the risk of respiratory infection
Increased production of lysozyme in tears
Fewer pathogens able to enter the respiratory tract
Mucus traps pathogens and cilia sweep the mucus up and out of the airways (the mucociliary escalator). Damaged cilia mean mucus and trapped pathogens accumulate, increasing infection risk.
bio34a2-pb-6
Distinguish between a pathogen and an antigen, and give an example of each. (2 marks)

A pathogen is an agent that causes disease, e.g. the influenza virus or the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis; an antigen is a molecule (often a protein or glycoprotein) that is recognised by the immune system and can trigger an immune response, e.g. the haemagglutinin protein on the surface of the influenza virus.
bio34a2-pb-7
Describe two physical or chemical barriers a eucalyptus tree could use to prevent infection by a fungal pathogen. (2 marks)

Physical: thick bark or a waxy cuticle that blocks entry of fungal hyphae, and/or thick cellulose cell walls that are hard to penetrate; chemical: production of antimicrobial/antifungal compounds such as essential oils, or enzymes such as chitinase that break down fungal cell walls (any two, with at least a correct description of each).
bio34a2-pb-8
Explain how the acidic environment of the stomach acts as a barrier to infection. (2 marks)

Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid giving a pH of about 1.5–3.5; this low pH denatures proteins (including enzymes) of many ingested microorganisms, killing them before they can reach and colonise the intestines.
vce-bio34-pb-c1
Prions differ from all other pathogens because they:
Are the smallest cellular pathogens, with a membrane but no nucleus or ribosomes
Can only infect plants, because they need a cell wall to enter their host cells
Carry RNA instead of DNA, which they insert into the genome of the host cell
Contain no nucleic acid; they are misfolded proteins that cause normal proteins to misfold
Bacteria, fungi and protozoa are cellular; viruses contain nucleic acid; prions are protein only.
vce-bio34-innate-immunity: bio34a2-inn-1
Which statement best describes the innate immune response?
It is specific to particular antigens and produces memory cells
It only occurs after vaccination
It is carried out only by B and T lymphocytes
It is non-specific, responds rapidly and does not produce immunological memory

The innate response (second line of defence) responds to general features shared by many pathogens, acts within minutes to hours and does not create memory. Specificity and memory are features of adaptive immunity carried out by lymphocytes.
bio34a2-inn-2
Mast cells release histamine during an inflammatory response. The effect of histamine is to
engulf and digest bacteria
produce antibodies against the pathogen
cause vasodilation and increased permeability of capillaries
kill virus-infected cells by releasing perforin

Histamine causes vasodilation (redness, heat) and increased capillary permeability, allowing fluid, complement proteins and phagocytes to move into the infected tissue (swelling). Natural killer cells and cytotoxic T cells release perforin.
bio34a2-inn-3
Natural killer (NK) cells are able to recognise and destroy
cells that have abnormal or reduced MHC class I markers, such as virus-infected or cancerous cells
free bacteria in the blood
antibodies bound to antigens
only cells displaying MHC class II with antigen

NK cells detect cells with reduced or abnormal MHC I (common in virus-infected and cancer cells) and induce apoptosis by releasing perforin and granzymes. They are part of innate immunity and do not need prior sensitisation.
bio34a2-inn-4
Interferons are produced by
bacteria to protect themselves from viruses
mast cells to cause vasodilation
plasma cells to bind to viruses
virus-infected cells, and they signal neighbouring cells to increase their resistance to viral replication
Interferons are cytokines released by virus-infected host cells. They signal neighbouring uninfected cells to produce antiviral proteins, slowing the spread of the virus. They are not antibodies.
bio34a2-inn-5
A child's body temperature rises to 39 °C during a bacterial infection. Which statement best explains how fever helps fight infection?
Higher temperature denatures all of the child's own enzymes
Higher temperature can slow bacterial reproduction and speed up some immune processes such as phagocytosis
Fever directly produces antibodies
Fever causes the skin to become impermeable to bacteria

A moderate fever, triggered by chemicals acting on the hypothalamus, creates conditions less favourable for many pathogens to reproduce and enhances some immune responses. Very high fevers can be harmful, but 39 °C does not denature most human enzymes.
bio34a2-inn-6
Describe the process of phagocytosis by a neutrophil. (3 marks)

The neutrophil is attracted to the infection site by chemical signals (chemotaxis) and recognises the pathogen (e.g. via receptors that bind pathogen surface molecules or complement/antibody); it engulfs the pathogen by extending its membrane around it, forming a phagosome (endocytosis); the phagosome fuses with a lysosome and hydrolytic enzymes digest the pathogen, with waste removed by exocytosis.
bio34a2-inn-7
A person steps on a rusty nail and the area becomes red, hot, swollen and painful. Explain how the inflammatory response produces these signs and how it helps clear the infection. (3 marks)

Damaged cells and mast cells release histamine and other chemicals; histamine causes vasodilation, increasing blood flow (redness and heat), and increases capillary permeability so fluid leaks into tissue (swelling, pressing on nerves to cause pain); increased permeability allows phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages) and complement proteins to move into the tissue and destroy pathogens, with clotting factors helping to wall off the area.
bio34a2-inn-8
Describe two ways the complement system helps to defend against bacterial infection. (2 marks)

Complement proteins can form a membrane attack complex that creates pores in the bacterial membrane, causing lysis; they can coat (opsonise) bacteria, making them easier for phagocytes to recognise and engulf; they also act as chemical signals that attract phagocytes to the site (any two).
vce-bio34-ii-c1
Which sequence best describes inflammation after a splinter breaks the skin?
Phagocytes release histamine → vessels constrict and become less permeable → antibodies move into the tissue
Mast cells release histamine → vessels dilate and become more permeable → phagocytes move into the tissue
B cells release histamine → vessels dilate and become more permeable → plasma cells move into the tissue
Mast cells release antibodies → vessels constrict → complement proteins move out of the tissue
Histamine causes vasodilation (redness, heat) and leaky capillaries (swelling), letting phagocytes and complement reach the site.
vce-bio34-antigen-presentation-and-the-l: bio34a2-ap-1
MHC class I markers are found on
only antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells
red blood cells only
all nucleated body cells
bacterial cells only

MHC I markers are present on all nucleated cells and display fragments of proteins made inside the cell (self or, if infected, viral peptides). MHC II is restricted to antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells. Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus and MHC I.
bio34a2-ap-2
After engulfing a pathogen in the skin, a dendritic cell travels to the nearest lymph node. The main purpose of this migration is to
present antigen fragments on MHC II to T helper cells with complementary receptors
produce antibodies in the lymph node
destroy the lymph node's B cells
release histamine into the lymph

Dendritic cells are antigen-presenting cells that carry antigen through lymphatic vessels to lymph nodes, where many naive T cells are concentrated. There, a T helper cell with a complementary receptor binds the MHC II–antigen complex and is activated.
bio34a2-ap-3
Which of the following is a function of the lymphatic system?
Pumping blood around the body
Filtering urea from the blood
Producing red blood cells in the lymph nodes
Returning excess tissue fluid to the blood and providing sites where lymphocytes encounter antigens

The lymphatic system collects excess tissue fluid (lymph) and returns it to the bloodstream, and its lymph nodes and spleen are secondary lymphoid tissues where lymphocytes are activated. It has no pump and does not make red blood cells.
bio34a2-ap-4
During an infection, a patient's lymph nodes in the neck become swollen and tender. This is most likely because
the lymph nodes are being destroyed by the pathogen
the lymphatic vessels have become blocked by mucus
red blood cells are accumulating in the nodes
lymphocytes in the nodes are undergoing clonal expansion after encountering antigen

When lymphocytes with receptors complementary to an antigen are activated in a lymph node, they proliferate rapidly (clonal expansion), increasing the size of the node. Swollen nodes are a sign that the adaptive response is under way.
bio34a2-ap-5
Where do B lymphocytes and T lymphocytes respectively mature?
B cells in the bone marrow; T cells in the thymus
Both mature in the thymus
B cells in the thymus; T cells in the bone marrow
Both mature in the lymph nodes
Both B and T cells originate from stem cells in bone marrow. B cells mature in the bone marrow, while T cells migrate to and mature in the thymus. Both are primary lymphoid organs.
bio34a2-ap-6
Compare MHC class I and MHC class II markers in terms of the cells that carry them and the source of the antigens they present. (3 marks)

MHC I is found on all nucleated cells, whereas MHC II is found only on antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); MHC I presents peptides from proteins made inside the cell (endogenous, e.g. viral proteins in an infected cell), which are recognised by cytotoxic T cells; MHC II presents peptides from material engulfed from outside the cell (exogenous, e.g. phagocytosed bacteria), which are recognised by T helper cells.
bio34a2-ap-7
Explain why tissues from an unrelated donor are often rejected after an organ transplant. (2 marks)

Cells of the donor organ carry MHC markers (self-markers) that differ from those of the recipient; the recipient's immune system recognises the donor MHC as non-self/foreign (antigens), activating T cells (and antibodies) that attack and destroy the transplanted tissue.
bio34a2-ap-8
Describe the role of the lymphatic system in the initiation of an adaptive immune response to bacteria entering a cut in the hand. (3 marks)

Bacteria and/or antigen-presenting cells such as dendritic cells that have engulfed the bacteria travel in lymph through lymphatic vessels; they reach a nearby lymph node, where the dendritic cell presents antigen on MHC II to T helper cells, and B cells encounter antigen; lymphocytes with complementary receptors are selected and undergo clonal expansion in the node, after which effector cells and antibodies leave via lymph and blood to the site of infection.
vce-bio34-ap-c1
Malaria parasites inside mature red blood cells cannot be detected by cytotoxic T cells mainly because:
Red blood cells display only MHC class II, which cytotoxic T cells ignore
Cytotoxic T cells cannot enter blood vessels, so they never meet red blood cells
Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and do not display MHC class I
Antibodies coat the parasite inside the cell, hiding it from T cells
Cytotoxic T cells recognise antigen presented on MHC I, which nucleated cells display. Mature red blood cells lack nuclei and MHC I.
vce-bio34-humoral-immunity: bio34a2-hum-1
Humoral immunity is primarily directed against
viruses replicating inside host cells
cancerous cells displaying abnormal MHC I
pathogens and antigens in extracellular fluids such as blood and lymph
transplanted tissue only

The humoral response produces antibodies that circulate in body fluids and act on extracellular pathogens and toxins. Infected and cancerous cells are targeted by cell-mediated immunity (cytotoxic T cells).
bio34a2-hum-2
During the humoral response, a B cell that has bound its specific antigen is fully activated when
it is engulfed by a macrophage
a T helper cell recognises the antigen presented on the B cell's MHC II and releases cytokines
it binds to an MHC I marker on an infected cell
a mast cell releases histamine

The B cell internalises the antigen and presents fragments on MHC II. A T helper cell with a complementary receptor binds and releases cytokines (e.g. interleukins), stimulating the B cell to undergo clonal expansion and differentiation.
bio34a2-hum-3
The part of an antibody that binds to a specific antigen is the
constant region of the heavy chain
hinge region
disulfide bridge between the heavy chains
variable region at the tips of the heavy and light chains

Each antibody has two antigen-binding sites formed by the variable regions of a heavy and a light chain. Differences in amino acid sequence here give each antibody its specificity. The constant region determines the antibody class and its interactions with other immune components.
bio34a2-hum-4
Antibodies bind to the spike proteins of a virus, preventing the virus from attaching to receptors on host cells. This mode of action is called
agglutination
opsonisation
neutralisation
lysis

Neutralisation occurs when antibodies cover the parts of a pathogen or toxin needed to bind host cells. Agglutination is the clumping of pathogens by antibodies; opsonisation is coating pathogens to enhance phagocytosis.
bio34a2-hum-5

A graph shows antibody concentration after a first and second exposure to the same antigen. Compared with the primary response, the secondary response is faster and produces a much higher antibody concentration. This is mainly due to
memory B cells produced during the first exposure rapidly differentiating into plasma cells
more mast cells being present after the first exposure
the antigen becoming weaker over time
antibodies from the first response remaining at high levels indefinitely

During the primary response, clonal expansion produces memory B cells as well as plasma cells. On re-exposure, the larger population of memory B cells responds quickly, differentiating into plasma cells that produce more antibody, sooner.
bio34a2-hum-6
Outline the sequence of events in the humoral immune response, from a naive B cell encountering an antigen to the production of antibodies. (4 marks)

A naive B cell with B cell receptors (membrane-bound antibodies) complementary to the antigen binds it (clonal selection) and presents antigen fragments on MHC II; a T helper cell that has been activated against the same antigen binds the B cell and releases cytokines; the B cell is stimulated to undergo clonal expansion (rapid mitosis), producing many identical cells; these differentiate into plasma cells, which secrete large quantities of specific antibodies, and memory B cells, which persist and provide a faster secondary response.
bio34a2-hum-7
Describe how antibodies can promote the destruction of bacteria by agglutination and opsonisation. (2 marks)

Agglutination: each antibody has (at least) two binding sites, so antibodies bind several bacteria at once, clumping them together so they cannot spread and are more easily engulfed by phagocytes; opsonisation: antibodies coat the bacteria and phagocytes recognise the constant region of bound antibodies, which increases the rate of phagocytosis.
bio34a2-hum-8
Explain why the antibodies produced against the measles virus do not protect against the chickenpox virus. (2 marks)

Antibodies are specific: the variable region of each antibody has a shape complementary to one specific antigen (epitope); antigens on the chickenpox virus have a different shape from measles antigens, so measles antibodies cannot bind to them, and no memory cells specific for chickenpox exist.
vce-bio34-hi-c1
A person has very few helper T cells (for example in advanced HIV infection). The most likely effect is:
Only innate immunity is affected, because helper T cells activate phagocytes
Antibody production increases to make up for the loss of helper T cells
Only cell-mediated immunity is affected, while B cells work as normal
Both antibody production and cytotoxic T cell responses are greatly weakened
Helper T cells release cytokines that activate the selected B cells (clonal expansion into plasma and memory cells) and cytotoxic T cells.
vce-bio34-cell-mediated-immunity: bio34a3-cmi-1
Which cell directly destroys a virus-infected body cell during cell-mediated immunity?
Plasma cell
Cytotoxic T cell
Helper T cell
Mast cell

Cytotoxic T cells recognise antigen presented on MHC I of infected cells and induce apoptosis. Plasma cells secrete antibodies (humoral immunity) and helper T cells coordinate the response but do not kill infected cells themselves.
bio34a3-cmi-2
A cytotoxic T cell recognises an infected cell because the infected cell displays
viral antigen fragments on MHC class II markers.
antibodies bound to its plasma membrane.
viral antigen fragments on MHC class I markers.
complement proteins in its cytosol.

Almost all nucleated cells display endogenous (internal) antigen fragments on MHC I, which is recognised by the T cell receptor and CD8 of cytotoxic T cells. MHC II is found on professional antigen-presenting cells and is recognised by helper T cells.
bio34a3-cmi-3
Perforin and granzymes released by a cytotoxic T cell cause the target cell to
undergo apoptosis.
be engulfed by a neutrophil immediately.
secrete interferon.
differentiate into a memory cell.

Perforin forms pores in the target cell membrane, allowing granzymes to enter and activate caspases, which trigger apoptosis (programmed cell death). Interferon is released by infected cells, not as a result of granzyme action.
bio34a3-cmi-4
A patient has a condition in which very few helper T cells are produced. Which outcome is most likely?
Only cell-mediated immunity is impaired; antibody production is normal.
Neither clonal expansion of B cells nor activation of cytotoxic T cells occurs effectively.
Innate barriers such as skin and mucus stop functioning.
The patient's cells stop expressing MHC I markers.

Helper T cells release cytokines (interleukins) that stimulate clonal expansion and differentiation of both selected B cells and cytotoxic T cells, so both arms of adaptive immunity are weakened (as in advanced HIV infection). Innate barriers and MHC expression are not dependent on helper T cells.
bio34a3-cmi-5
Following an infection, a small number of cytotoxic T cells persist for years and produce a faster response if the same antigen is encountered again. These cells are
regulatory T cells.
naive T cells.
plasma cells.
memory T cells.

Memory T cells are produced during clonal expansion and persist long-term, enabling a faster, larger secondary response. Plasma cells are antibody-secreting B cell derivatives and naive T cells have not yet encountered their antigen.
bio34a3-cmi-6
Outline the sequence of events from the presentation of a viral antigen by a dendritic cell in a lymph node to the destruction of infected body cells by cytotoxic T cells. (4 marks)

Dendritic cell presents viral antigen on MHC II to a helper T cell with a complementary T cell receptor (and antigen on MHC I to a naive cytotoxic T cell with a complementary receptor); the activated helper T cell releases cytokines/interleukins; cytokines stimulate clonal selection and clonal expansion of the specific cytotoxic T cells (and production of memory T cells); cytotoxic T cells leave the lymph node, travel to the infection site, bind infected cells displaying the antigen on MHC I and release perforin and granzymes, causing apoptosis.
bio34a3-cmi-7
Explain why cell-mediated immunity, rather than humoral immunity, is required to eliminate a virus once it is inside host cells. (2 marks)

Antibodies are found in body fluids (plasma, lymph) and can only bind antigens/pathogens outside cells, so they cannot reach viruses replicating inside cells; cytotoxic T cells recognise viral antigen displayed on MHC I of infected cells and destroy the whole infected cell, removing the site of viral replication.
bio34a3-cmi-8
Organ transplant recipients are given drugs that suppress T cell activity. Explain why these drugs are needed and identify one risk of taking them. (3 marks)

Donor cells display MHC markers that differ from the recipient's (non-self); recipient cytotoxic T cells (activated with help from helper T cells) would recognise these as foreign and destroy the transplanted tissue, causing rejection; suppressing T cells reduces rejection but increases the risk of infections (or certain cancers) because the recipient's adaptive immune response is weakened.
vce-bio34-cm-c1
Explain how a cytotoxic T cell destroys a virus-infected cell, and why antibodies alone cannot clear an established viral infection.

The infected cell presents viral antigen on MHC I. A cytotoxic T cell with a complementary receptor binds it and releases perforin and granzymes, triggering apoptosis. Antibodies act only outside cells, and viruses replicating inside cells are hidden from them.
Mention MHC I, receptor specificity, apoptosis, and the location of the virus.
vce-bio34-types-of-immunity-and-vaccinat: bio34a3-tiv-1
A newborn receives antibodies from its mother through breast milk. This is an example of
natural active immunity.
natural passive immunity.
artificial passive immunity.
artificial active immunity.

The antibodies are received naturally (not by medical intervention) and made by another individual, so it is natural passive immunity. Active immunity requires the person's own B cells to make antibodies and memory cells.
bio34a3-tiv-2
A bushwalker bitten by an eastern brown snake is given antivenom. Which statement about this treatment is correct?
It provides long-lasting protection because memory B cells are produced.
It stimulates the bushwalker's plasma cells to make antivenom antibodies.
It provides immediate but short-term protection.
It is an example of artificial active immunity.

Antivenom contains pre-made antibodies, giving artificial passive immunity: it acts immediately but no memory cells are formed, and the antibodies are broken down within weeks. The bushwalker's own B cells are not involved.
bio34a3-tiv-3
Which of the following best explains why a second dose (booster) of a vaccine is often given?
To trigger a secondary response that produces more memory cells and a higher antibody level.
To replace the antibodies passively transferred by the first dose.
To activate the innate immune system for the first time.
To reduce the number of memory cells so that autoimmunity is avoided.

A booster exposes memory cells to the antigen again, producing a faster, larger secondary response with higher antibody titres and more memory cells, extending protection. Vaccines produce active, not passive, immunity.
bio34a3-tiv-4
An mRNA vaccine against a virus works by
inserting viral genes into the recipient's chromosomes.
delivering live but weakened virus particles to body cells.
supplying ready-made antibodies against the viral spike protein.
causing the recipient's cells to translate a viral antigen, which then stimulates an adaptive immune response.

mRNA in lipid nanoparticles enters cells and is translated into a viral protein (antigen), which is presented to lymphocytes, stimulating antibody production and memory cells. mRNA does not enter the nucleus or integrate into DNA, and it is not an attenuated or passive vaccine.
bio34a3-tiv-5
In a town, 95% of people are vaccinated against measles. An unvaccinated infant in the town is unlikely to catch measles mainly because
the infant has natural active immunity from birth.
the chain of transmission is broken, as most contacts cannot become infected.
the measles virus cannot infect infants.
vaccinated people pass antibodies to unvaccinated people by contact.

This is herd immunity: when a high proportion of the population is immune, the pathogen cannot spread efficiently, protecting those who cannot be vaccinated. Antibodies are not transferred by casual contact.
bio34a3-tiv-6
Distinguish between active and passive immunity, referring to the duration of protection in each. (3 marks)

Active immunity: the individual's own immune system is exposed to an antigen and produces antibodies (via plasma cells) and memory cells; protection is long-lasting because of memory cells (but takes time to develop); passive immunity: antibodies made by another organism are received, giving immediate protection; it is short-lived because no memory cells are made and the antibodies are degraded.
bio34a3-tiv-7

A graph shows antibody concentration in a person's blood over 60 days. A vaccine was given on day 0 and a booster on day 30. Antibody levels peaked at a low level around day 12 and then declined; after day 30 they rose more quickly to a peak about ten times higher. Explain the difference between the two responses. (3 marks)

The first dose triggered a primary response: naive B cells had to undergo clonal selection and expansion, so there was a lag and a small peak; memory B cells (and memory helper T cells) were produced during the primary response; at the booster, these memory cells recognised the antigen and rapidly differentiated into many plasma cells, producing a faster and much larger secondary response.
bio34a3-tiv-8
Explain why vaccination rates below the herd immunity threshold can lead to an outbreak, even though most people are vaccinated. (2 marks)

If fewer people are immune than the threshold, an infected person is likely to contact enough susceptible people that each case leads to more than one new case; the pathogen can then spread through clusters of susceptible (unvaccinated or non-responding) individuals, causing an outbreak.
vce-bio34-tv-c1
The herd immunity threshold is about 1 − 1/R₀. For measles, R₀ ≈ 15. Roughly what proportion of a population must be immune?
About 93%
About 15%
About 50%
About 67%
1 − 1/15 ≈ 0.93. Highly infectious diseases need very high vaccination coverage.
vce-bio34-emerging-diseases-and-immunoth: bio34a3-edi-1
Which of the following is an example of a re-emerging disease?
A disease caused by a newly identified coronavirus that jumped from bats to humans
Measles returning to a region after vaccination rates fall
A genetic disorder caused by a new point mutation
Type 2 diabetes increasing with age

A re-emerging disease is a known disease that had declined but is increasing again, e.g. measles after falling vaccination rates. A new coronavirus jumping species is an emerging disease; genetic and lifestyle conditions are not infectious diseases.
bio34a3-edi-2
Which factor most directly increases the speed at which a new infectious disease spreads between countries?
International air travel
Improved sanitation
Higher vaccination coverage
Antibiotic stewardship programs
Air travel allows infected people to move between continents within the incubation period, spreading the pathogen rapidly, as occurred with COVID-19. The other options reduce disease spread.
bio34a3-edi-3
Monoclonal antibodies are produced by
injecting a patient with weakened pathogens.
isolating antibodies from the blood of many different donors.
fusing a specific plasma (B) cell with a myeloma (cancer) cell to form a hybridoma that is cloned.
inserting antibody genes into memory T cells.

A hybridoma combines the ability of a plasma cell to make one specific antibody with the ability of a myeloma cell to divide indefinitely; clones produce identical (monoclonal) antibodies. Pooled donor antibodies would be polyclonal.
bio34a3-edi-4

Some cancer cells display the protein PD-L1, which binds to PD-1 on cytotoxic T cells and switches them off. A monoclonal antibody that binds PD-1 is used as a treatment. This works because the antibody
kills the cancer cells directly by causing apoptosis.
prevents PD-L1 from binding, so cytotoxic T cells remain active against the cancer cells.
binds PD-L1 and marks cancer cells for destruction by complement.
stimulates B cells to produce antibodies against PD-1.

This is a checkpoint inhibitor: blocking PD-1 stops the cancer cell's PD-L1 from inactivating the T cell, so the patient's cytotoxic T cells can recognise and destroy the cancer. The antibody targets PD-1 on T cells, not PD-L1 on cancer cells, and does not itself kill cells.
bio34a3-edi-5

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have long used plants such as the gumby gumby (Pittosporum angustifolium) for medicinal purposes. The most appropriate way for researchers to investigate such plants for new drugs is to
collect plants from Country without consultation, as plants are a public resource.
patent traditional knowledge so that communities cannot use it commercially.
partner with Traditional Owners, gain free, prior and informed consent and share benefits.
rely solely on written colonial records of plant use.
Ethical research respects Indigenous cultural and intellectual property, involving genuine partnership, informed consent and benefit-sharing with the communities who hold the knowledge.
bio34a3-edi-6
Identify two factors that contributed to the rapid global spread of COVID-19 and explain how each increased transmission. (4 marks)

Factor 1: international travel/globalisation; infected people (including asymptomatic carriers) moved between countries before detection, seeding new outbreaks; factor 2: high population density/urbanisation or a lack of prior immunity in the population; crowded conditions increase contact rates for airborne/droplet spread, and with no existing immunity (novel virus) almost everyone was susceptible. (Accept also asymptomatic transmission, long incubation period.)
bio34a3-edi-7
Explain how a monoclonal antibody that binds a protein found only on the surface of breast cancer cells can be used to treat the cancer. (3 marks)

The monoclonal antibody is specific/complementary to the antigen (e.g. HER2) on the cancer cell, so it binds only cancer cells and not healthy cells; binding may block the receptor and stop signals that stimulate uncontrolled division; it can also tag the cell for destruction by immune cells (e.g. NK cells/phagocytes), or carry an attached drug/radioactive substance directly to the cancer cell.
bio34a3-edi-8
Explain how a zoonotic pathogen can become an emerging human disease. (2 marks)

A pathogen that normally infects animals (reservoir host) is transmitted to humans through close contact, e.g. habitat destruction, wildlife trade or farming; mutation(s) may allow the pathogen to bind human cells and spread from human to human, and because humans have no prior immunity it can spread rapidly.
vce-bio34-ed-c1
Some cancer cells display PD-L1, which binds PD-1 on T cells and switches them off. A monoclonal antibody against PD-1 helps treat cancer by:
Blocking PD-1 so T cells stay active and attack the cancer cells
Binding to the T cells and destroying them, so they stop attacking
Entering the cancer cells and directly digesting their DNA
Giving the patient memory B cells against the cancer antigen
Checkpoint inhibitors release the brakes on the patient's own T cells. This is immunotherapy, a form of passive treatment, not vaccination.
vce-bio34-mutations-gene-flow-and-geneti: bio34a3-mgd-1
Which of the following is the only source of entirely new alleles in a population?
Mutation
Gene flow
Genetic drift
Natural selection

Mutation changes DNA sequences and creates new alleles. Gene flow can introduce alleles that are new to a particular population, but they already existed elsewhere; drift and selection only change existing allele frequencies.
bio34a3-mgd-2
A deletion of a single nucleotide near the start of a gene is likely to have a greater effect than a substitution because it
changes only one amino acid.
always produces a silent mutation.
causes a frameshift that alters every codon downstream.
removes the promoter from the gene.
Deleting one base shifts the reading frame, so all downstream codons are changed, often producing a non-functional protein or an early stop codon. A substitution affects at most one codon.
bio34a3-mgd-3
Tasmanian devil populations have extremely low genetic diversity, which is thought to have resulted from population crashes thousands of years ago. This is best described as
the founder effect.
gene flow.
a bottleneck effect.
artificial selection.

A bottleneck occurs when a population is drastically reduced, so the surviving gene pool is a small, random sample of the original, reducing diversity. The founder effect involves a small group colonising a new area.
bio34a3-mgd-4
Which population is most likely to experience large changes in allele frequency due to genetic drift?
A population of 10 000 frogs with frequent migration
A population of 25 rock-wallabies isolated on an island
A population of 50 000 mosquitoes
A population of 5000 grasses with wind-borne pollen from other populations

Genetic drift is random change in allele frequency and has the greatest effect in small, isolated populations, where chance events strongly change the proportions of alleles passed on. Gene flow counteracts drift.
bio34a3-mgd-5
Pollen from genetically modified canola is carried by wind into a neighbouring population of wild canola, where it fertilises some plants. The effect on the wild population is
genetic drift, which increases genetic differences between the populations.
a bottleneck, which reduces diversity.
mutation, which creates new alleles in the GM crop.
gene flow, which makes the gene pools of the two populations more similar.
Movement of alleles between populations via gametes (pollen) is gene flow; it tends to make populations more genetically similar. No new mutation occurs in this process.
bio34a3-mgd-6
Distinguish between the founder effect and the bottleneck effect, and state one similarity. (3 marks)

Founder effect: a small group of individuals leaves a population to colonise a new area, so the new population's gene pool reflects only the founders' alleles; bottleneck effect: a large population is drastically reduced in size by a chance event (e.g. bushfire, disease), and survivors carry only a subset of alleles; similarity: both are forms of genetic drift that reduce genetic diversity and can change allele frequencies by chance.
bio34a3-mgd-7

A population of 200 skinks has an allele frequency of 0.4 for allele B. After a flood kills 180 skinks at random, the frequency of B in the survivors is 0.15. Identify the mechanism responsible and explain why the change occurred. (2 marks)

Genetic drift (a bottleneck effect); because the deaths were random rather than related to phenotype, the 20 survivors happened by chance to carry fewer B alleles, so the allele frequency changed without selection.
bio34a3-mgd-8
Explain how a mutation in a somatic cell differs from a mutation in a germline cell in its significance for the evolution of a population. (2 marks)

A somatic mutation occurs in a body cell and is not passed to offspring, so it cannot change the population's gene pool; a germline mutation occurs in cells that produce gametes and can be inherited, introducing a new allele into the gene pool on which evolutionary mechanisms can act.
vce-bio34-mg-c1
Twenty birds colonise an island. One allele has a frequency of 0.6 on the island but 0.3 on the mainland. This is best explained by:
Gene flow between the island and the mainland
The founder effect, a form of genetic drift
Natural selection for the allele
A new mutation on the island
A small founding group carries a non-representative sample of alleles by chance. Gene flow would make the frequencies more similar.
vce-bio34-natural-selection-and-selectiv: bio34a3-nss-1
Which of the following is NOT a requirement for evolution by natural selection?
Heritable variation in a trait within the population
A selection pressure in the environment
Individuals deliberately changing their traits to suit the environment
Differential survival and reproduction
Natural selection acts on existing heritable variation; individuals cannot choose to acquire inherited traits. Variation, a selection pressure and differential reproduction are all required.
bio34a3-nss-2
Cane toads at the invasion front in northern Australia have longer legs than toads in long-established populations. The most likely explanation is that
toads stretch their legs while travelling, and this is passed to offspring.
longer-legged toads disperse faster, reach new areas first and breed with other fast toads.
longer legs arose by mutation because toads needed to move faster.
genetic drift always increases leg length in amphibians.

At the front, toads with heritable longer legs travel further and arrive first, so they breed together and pass on the alleles, increasing their frequency (spatial sorting/selection). Acquired characteristics are not inherited, and mutations do not arise in response to need.
bio34a3-nss-3
Compared with natural selection, selective breeding of dairy cattle
involves humans choosing which individuals reproduce, often reducing genetic diversity.
increases genetic diversity because only the best animals breed.
does not change allele frequencies in the population.
relies on random mutations being caused by the farmer.
In selective breeding, humans are the selecting agent and breed individuals with desired traits, which increases desired allele frequencies but narrows the gene pool, reducing diversity.
bio34a3-nss-4
A population of moths contains dark and light forms. After a fire blackens tree bark, the frequency of the dark allele increases over several generations. The selection pressure is
the mutation producing dark colour.
the dark colour of the moths.
the reduced genetic diversity.
predation by birds that see contrasting moths more easily.
The selection pressure is the environmental factor that affects survival: birds preferentially eat moths that contrast with the bark. The dark colour is the advantageous phenotype, not the pressure.
bio34a3-nss-5
Which is a likely disadvantage of a crop variety produced by many generations of selective breeding?
It always produces a lower yield.
It cannot be grown in Australia.
Plants are genetically very similar, so the whole crop may be vulnerable to a single new disease.
It contains more alleles than the wild type.
Selective breeding narrows genetic diversity; with uniform genotypes, a pathogen able to infect one plant can infect most of the crop, risking total crop failure.
bio34a3-nss-6

Using the example of a population of algae-eating snails in which some individuals have thicker shells, explain how natural selection could increase the frequency of thick shells after crabs are introduced as predators. (4 marks)

Variation: snails in the population vary in shell thickness due to different alleles (arising from mutation); selection pressure: crabs crush and eat thin-shelled snails more easily; selective advantage: thick-shelled snails are more likely to survive and reproduce; inheritance: they pass the thick-shell alleles to offspring, so over many generations the frequency of the thick-shell allele/phenotype increases in the population.
bio34a3-nss-7
Explain why selective breeding can produce large phenotypic changes in a species in far fewer generations than natural selection usually does. (2 marks)

Humans apply a strong, consistent and deliberate selection pressure, allowing only individuals with the desired trait to breed each generation; in natural selection, pressures vary and individuals without the advantageous trait still often reproduce, so allele frequencies change more slowly.
bio34a3-nss-8
A farmer breeds sheep for fine wool for 30 generations. Describe the likely effect on the genetic diversity of the flock and explain one consequence. (2 marks)

Genetic diversity decreases because only a few sheep with particular alleles are used for breeding (and inbreeding increases); consequence: the flock has a reduced ability to adapt to environmental change/disease, or recessive harmful conditions become more common due to increased homozygosity.
vce-bio34-ns-c1
Why are crops produced by intensive selective breeding often more vulnerable to new diseases?
Selection for a few traits reduces genetic diversity, so fewer individuals may carry resistance alleles
Selective breeding causes new harmful mutations, so the crops are weaker against pathogens
Natural selection stops acting on crops, so they cannot evolve resistance to anything
Bred crops have fewer chromosomes, so they carry fewer genes for fighting disease
Low diversity means one pathogen can affect most of the population, as in the Irish potato famine.
vce-bio34-antibiotic-and-antiviral-resis: bio34a3-aar-1
Which statement correctly describes the development of antibiotic resistance in a bacterial population?
Bacteria develop resistance because they are exposed to the antibiotic and need to survive.
The antibiotic causes the mutation that makes bacteria resistant.
Resistant bacteria already present survive the antibiotic and reproduce, increasing the frequency of resistance.
Patients become resistant to the antibiotic after repeated use.

Resistance alleles arise by random mutation (or are acquired by horizontal gene transfer) before exposure; the antibiotic acts as a selection pressure, killing susceptible bacteria. Bacteria, not patients, become resistant.
bio34a3-aar-2
Bacteria can rapidly share resistance genes with other bacteria, including other species, through
meiosis.
transfer of plasmids by conjugation.
binary fission.
antigen presentation.

Horizontal gene transfer via plasmids (conjugation) spreads resistance genes between bacteria. Binary fission passes genes only to daughter cells (vertical transfer), and bacteria do not undergo meiosis.
bio34a3-aar-3
Why does failing to complete a prescribed course of antibiotics contribute to resistance?
It allows the more-resistant bacteria that survived early doses to multiply.
It causes the patient's immune cells to become resistant.
It converts the antibiotic into a mutagen.
It increases gene flow between the patient and other people.
Early doses kill the most susceptible bacteria; stopping early leaves those with partial resistance alive to reproduce, so resistance alleles increase in frequency.
bio34a3-aar-4

Influenza viruses with a mutation in the neuraminidase gene are not inhibited by the antiviral drug oseltamivir (Tamiflu). In a hospital where oseltamivir is widely used, the proportion of resistant viruses would be expected to
decrease, as the drug destroys the mutated gene.
stay the same, as viruses do not evolve.
decrease, because viruses cannot mutate.
increase, as the drug selects for viruses with the mutation.

The drug is a selection pressure: susceptible viruses are inhibited while resistant variants replicate and spread, increasing their frequency. Viruses evolve rapidly because of high mutation rates and short replication times.
bio34a3-aar-5
Which practice would be most effective in slowing the evolution of antibiotic resistance in Australia?
Prescribing antibiotics for viral colds as a precaution
Using broad-spectrum antibiotics routinely in livestock feed to promote growth
Prescribing antibiotics only for bacterial infections, using narrow-spectrum drugs where possible
Using a single antibiotic for all infections

Reducing unnecessary use lowers the selection pressure for resistance. Antibiotics are ineffective against viruses, and routine use in livestock and relying on one drug increase selection for resistance.
bio34a3-aar-6
Explain how a population of Staphylococcus aureus in a hospital could become resistant to methicillin (MRSA) over time. (4 marks)

Variation: some bacteria possess a resistance allele/gene that arose by random mutation or was acquired by plasmid transfer; selection pressure: methicillin use kills susceptible bacteria; resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly by binary fission, passing on the resistance gene (and may share it by conjugation); over many generations the frequency of resistant bacteria increases until most of the population is resistant.
bio34a3-aar-7
HIV is treated with a combination of three antiviral drugs that act on different targets rather than one drug. Explain why. (2 marks)

For a virus to survive, it would need resistance mutations to all three drugs at once, which is extremely unlikely; so combination therapy reduces the chance that resistant variants survive and are selected, slowing the evolution of resistance.
bio34a3-aar-8
Explain why antibiotic resistance can evolve in bacteria within months, whereas changes in human populations take thousands of years. (2 marks)

Bacteria have very short generation times (can divide every 20–30 minutes) and huge population sizes, so mutations arise frequently and selection acts over many generations quickly; humans have long generation times and fewer offspring, so changes in allele frequency take much longer.
vce-bio34-ar-c1
Explain how resistance to an antibiotic arises in a bacterial population, and why stopping a course early can make it worse.

Random mutations already give a few bacteria some resistance. The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, so resistant ones survive and reproduce, passing on the allele (natural selection). Stopping early leaves the more resistant survivors to multiply.
The antibiotic does not cause the mutation; it selects for it. Horizontal gene transfer (plasmids) can spread resistance too.
vce-bio34-speciation: bio34a3-spe-1
According to the biological species concept, two organisms belong to the same species if they
look very similar.
live in the same habitat.
have exactly the same DNA sequence.
can interbreed under natural conditions to produce viable, fertile offspring.

The biological species concept is based on reproductive compatibility producing viable, fertile offspring. Similar appearance and shared habitat are not sufficient, and individuals within a species have different DNA sequences.
bio34a3-spe-2
Which sequence correctly describes allopatric speciation?
Geographical isolation → different selection pressures and genetic drift → genetic divergence → reproductive isolation
Reproductive isolation → geographical isolation → gene flow → new species
Mutation → gene flow → interbreeding → new species
Polyploidy → hybridisation → geographical isolation → new species

A geographical barrier prevents gene flow; each population experiences different selection pressures, mutations and drift, so gene pools diverge until the populations can no longer interbreed even if brought together.
bio34a3-spe-3
A horse and a donkey can mate to produce a mule, which is sterile. This shows that horses and donkeys
are the same species, as they can mate.
are separate species, as their hybrid offspring are not fertile.
are undergoing sympatric speciation right now.
have no shared ancestor.
Mules are infertile, so horses and donkeys cannot produce fertile offspring and are separate species (post-zygotic isolation). Their ability to hybridise reflects a relatively recent common ancestor.
bio34a3-spe-4
Two populations of frogs live in the same pond, but one breeds in early spring and the other in late summer. This is an example of
geographical isolation.
gene flow.
temporal (seasonal) reproductive isolation.
hybrid sterility.
Breeding at different times prevents interbreeding even though the populations share a habitat; this is a pre-zygotic temporal isolating mechanism, which can lead to sympatric speciation.
bio34a3-spe-5
Sympatric speciation in plants often occurs through polyploidy because
polyploid plants are geographically separated from the parent population.
polyploidy increases gene flow with the parent population.
polyploid plants always have lower fitness and die out.
a polyploid plant cannot produce fertile offspring with the parent species, so it is instantly reproductively isolated.

A polyploid (e.g. tetraploid) crossed with a diploid parent produces triploid offspring that are usually sterile because chromosomes cannot pair in meiosis, so the polyploid is reproductively isolated in the same location.
bio34a3-spe-6
Around 10 000 years ago, rising sea levels separated Kangaroo Island from mainland South Australia. Explain how this could lead to the formation of a new species of wallaby on the island. (4 marks)

Rising sea level created a geographical barrier, so gene flow between island and mainland populations stopped; the island population faced different selection pressures (e.g. climate, food, predators) and natural selection favoured different alleles; random mutations and genetic drift (small island population) further changed allele frequencies; over many generations the gene pools diverged so much that the populations would be reproductively isolated (unable to produce fertile offspring) if reunited, meaning a new species had formed (allopatric speciation).
bio34a3-spe-7
Distinguish between allopatric and sympatric speciation. (2 marks)

Allopatric speciation occurs when populations are separated by a geographical barrier that prevents gene flow; sympatric speciation occurs within the same geographical area, where reproductive isolation arises without a physical barrier (e.g. by polyploidy, behavioural or temporal isolation).
bio34a3-spe-8
Two populations of birds separated for 50 000 years are reunited. Describe an experiment or observation that would determine whether speciation has occurred. (2 marks)

Observe (or allow) the two populations to interbreed under natural conditions; if they do not mate or their offspring are not viable/fertile (e.g. test whether hybrid offspring can produce their own offspring), they are reproductively isolated and are separate species; if fertile offspring are produced, speciation has not occurred.
vce-bio34-sp-c1
Two frog populations can interbreed and produce fertile offspring in a laboratory but never do in the wild, because they breed at different times of year. This is:
Postzygotic isolation
Geographic isolation only
Evidence that they are one species, because they can interbreed
Temporal (prezygotic) isolation, and they can be regarded as separate species
The biological species concept asks whether populations interbreed in nature. Different breeding seasons are a prezygotic barrier.
vce-bio34-fossil-record-and-dating: bio34a3-frd-1
Which conditions most favour the formation of a fossil?
Exposure to oxygen and scavengers on the ground surface
Rapid burial in fine sediment with low oxygen
Slow decomposition in warm, moist soil with many bacteria
Remains left in a fast-flowing river bed of coarse gravel

Rapid burial in fine sediment (e.g. mud, volcanic ash) in anoxic conditions protects remains from scavengers, decomposers and oxygen, allowing mineralisation. Oxygen and decomposers break remains down.
bio34a3-frd-2
In an undisturbed sequence of sedimentary rock layers, fossil X is found in a lower layer than fossil Y. Which conclusion is valid?
Fossil X is younger than fossil Y.
Fossil X is older than fossil Y.
Fossil X is exactly twice the age of fossil Y.
Fossil X and fossil Y must be the same species.
The law of superposition states that, in undisturbed strata, lower layers were deposited earlier and are older. This is relative dating, which gives order but not an absolute age.
bio34a3-frd-3
Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5730 years. A bone sample contains one-eighth of the carbon-14 expected in living tissue. The approximate age of the bone is
5730 years.
11 460 years.
17 190 years.
45 840 years.
One-eighth remaining = (1/2)³, so three half-lives have passed: 3 × 5730 = 17 190 years. Two half-lives (11 460 years) would leave one-quarter.
bio34a3-frd-4
Carbon-14 dating would NOT be suitable for determining the age of a 65-million-year-old dinosaur fossil because
dinosaurs did not contain carbon.
carbon-14 is only found in volcanic rock.
the half-life of carbon-14 is too short, so almost no carbon-14 would remain.
carbon-14 dating only works for plants.

Carbon-14 is useful up to about 50 000 years; after that too little remains to measure. Older fossils are dated by measuring isotopes with long half-lives (e.g. potassium-40 → argon-40) in volcanic layers above and below the fossil.
bio34a3-frd-5
Stromatolites at Shark Bay, Western Australia, are significant in the fossil record because
they are formed by cyanobacteria, and fossil stromatolites are among the oldest evidence of life (about 3.5 billion years).
they are the oldest fossils of multicellular animals.
they show the transition from fish to amphibians.
they are index fossils for the Jurassic period.

Stromatolites are layered structures built by cyanobacterial mats trapping sediment; fossil examples from the Pilbara are about 3.5 billion years old, and living Shark Bay stromatolites help scientists interpret them.
bio34a3-frd-6
Explain why the fossil record is incomplete. Give two reasons. (2 marks)

Fossilisation requires rare conditions (rapid burial, low oxygen), so most organisms decompose or are scavenged without forming fossils; soft-bodied organisms rarely fossilise; and many fossils are destroyed by erosion or geological activity, or have not yet been discovered. (Any two.)
bio34a3-frd-7

A fossil is found in a sedimentary layer between two volcanic ash layers. The ash layer above is dated at 3.2 million years and the ash layer below at 3.6 million years. Explain how these dates were obtained and what they tell us about the fossil. (3 marks)

The volcanic ash layers were dated by absolute (radiometric) dating, e.g. potassium-argon dating, which measures the ratio of a parent isotope to its stable daughter product and uses the known half-life; sedimentary rock itself cannot easily be dated this way; by superposition, the fossil is younger than the lower layer and older than the upper layer, so it is between 3.2 and 3.6 million years old.
bio34a3-frd-8
Define an index fossil and explain how it can be used to compare the ages of rock layers at two distant sites. (2 marks)

An index fossil is from a species that was widespread geographically but existed for a relatively short period of time; if the same index fossil is found in rock layers at both sites, the layers can be inferred to be of similar age (relative dating/correlation).
vce-bio34-fd-c1
Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years. A bone has 12.5% of the ¹⁴C expected in living tissue. Its approximate age is:
5730 years
17 190 years
11 460 years
45 840 years
12.5% = (1/2)³, so three half-lives: 3 × 5730 = 17 190 years. Dinosaur fossils are far too old for ¹⁴C dating.
vce-bio34-evidence-of-relatedness-and-ph: bio34a3-erp-1
The forelimbs of a human, a bat and a whale have the same arrangement of bones but different functions. These are
analogous structures, showing convergent evolution.
vestigial structures, showing loss of function.
homologous structures, showing divergent evolution from a common ancestor.
analogous structures, showing a common ancestor.

Homologous structures share the same underlying structure inherited from a common ancestor but have been modified for different functions (divergent evolution). Analogous structures have similar functions but different origins.
bio34a3-erp-2
The wings of a bird and the wings of an insect are best described as
homologous structures.
analogous structures.
vestigial structures.
transitional structures.
Bird and insect wings both enable flight but have entirely different structures and evolutionary origins, so they are analogous, resulting from convergent evolution under similar selection pressures.
bio34a3-erp-3
The table shows the number of amino acid differences in cytochrome c between humans and four other species: rhesus monkey 1, dog 11, kangaroo 10, yeast 44. Which conclusion is best supported?
Humans are most closely related to yeast.
Kangaroos are more closely related to humans than to dogs.
Humans share a more recent common ancestor with the rhesus monkey than with any of the other species listed.
Dogs and kangaroos are the same species.

The fewer amino acid differences, the more recent the common ancestor. Rhesus monkey has only 1 difference. The data compare each species with humans, so they do not show how kangaroos relate to dogs.
bio34a3-erp-4
On a phylogenetic tree, a node represents
a species that is now extinct with no descendants.
a common ancestor from which two or more lineages diverged.
the present-day species being compared.
the number of mutations in a gene.
Each node (branch point) represents a hypothetical common ancestor where lineages split. The tips of branches represent the taxa being compared.
bio34a3-erp-5
Why are comparisons of DNA sequences generally more reliable than comparisons of amino acid sequences for determining relatedness?
DNA sequences can be compared only in living species.
Amino acid sequences never change over time.
Proteins contain more information than genes.
DNA comparisons detect all changes, including silent mutations and non-coding regions that do not alter amino acids.

Because the genetic code is degenerate, some DNA changes do not change the amino acid sequence; DNA also includes non-coding regions. DNA comparisons therefore reveal more differences and give finer resolution of relatedness.
bio34a3-erp-6
Explain what vestigial structures are and why they provide evidence for evolution. Use an example. (3 marks)

Vestigial structures are reduced structures that have little or no function in the organism but were functional in its ancestors; example: the human coccyx (tailbone), or pelvic bones in whales/pythons; they provide evidence that the species shares a common ancestor with organisms in which the structure is functional, having been retained from that ancestor but reduced through evolution as it lost its selective advantage.
bio34a3-erp-7
A segment of a gene has the following number of base differences between four species: P–Q 2, P–R 8, P–S 9, Q–R 8, Q–S 9, R–S 4. Describe the phylogenetic tree these data support. (3 marks)

P and Q are most closely related (2 differences) and share the most recent common ancestor; R and S are more closely related to each other (4 differences) than to P or Q, forming a second group; the two groups (P+Q and R+S) diverged from an earlier common ancestor, at the base of the tree.
bio34a3-erp-8
The molecular clock assumes that mutations accumulate at a constant rate. Explain how this can be used to estimate when two species diverged, and state one limitation. (3 marks)

The number of DNA (or amino acid) differences between two species is counted; dividing by the known mutation rate (calibrated using fossils of known age) estimates the time since they shared a common ancestor; limitation: mutation rates can vary between genes, species and over time (e.g. due to generation time or selection), so estimates may be inaccurate.
vce-bio34-er-c1
Which pair of structures is evidence of divergent evolution from a common ancestor?
A human arm and a whale flipper
A bird wing and an insect wing
A shark fin and a dolphin flipper
An octopus eye and a human eye
Homologous structures share a bone pattern from a common ancestor but have different functions. The other pairs are analogous (convergent evolution).
vce-bio34-human-evolution: bio34a3-hev-1
Which feature of the skull most clearly indicates that a hominin walked upright (bipedal)?
A large brow ridge
A foramen magnum positioned centrally underneath the skull
A protruding jaw (prognathism)
Large canine teeth

A centrally placed foramen magnum allows the skull to balance on top of a vertical spine, indicating bipedalism. In quadrupedal apes it is positioned further back. The other features relate to diet or general morphology.
bio34a3-hev-2
Compared with the pelvis of a chimpanzee, the pelvis of a modern human is
long and narrow, to support knuckle-walking.
identical, as both are bipedal.
short, broad and bowl-shaped, supporting the internal organs and attachment of walking muscles.
fused with the femur.

The human pelvis is short and bowl-shaped, supporting abdominal organs during upright posture and positioning muscles for efficient bipedal walking. Chimpanzees have a long, narrow pelvis suited to quadrupedal locomotion.
bio34a3-hev-3

Analysis of DNA shows that many living people outside Africa carry about 1–2% Neanderthal DNA, and some populations (e.g. in Papua New Guinea and among Aboriginal Australians) also carry Denisovan DNA. This indicates that
Homo sapiens evolved from Neanderthals in Europe.
Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans after migrating out of Africa.
Neanderthals are the direct ancestors of Denisovans only.
Denisovans evolved in Australia.
Shared DNA segments indicate interbreeding (gene flow) between Homo sapiens and archaic hominins in Eurasia after the out-of-Africa migration. Homo sapiens evolved in Africa, not from Neanderthals.
bio34a3-hev-4
Archaeological evidence from Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land suggests that people have lived in Australia for at least about
5000 years.
10 000 years.
65 000 years.
2 million years.
Artefacts at Madjedbebe have been dated to around 65 000 years ago, supporting the long, continuous presence of Aboriginal peoples in Australia. Homo sapiens has existed for only about 300 000 years.
bio34a3-hev-5
The term 'hominin' refers to
all primates, including lemurs and monkeys.
all great apes, including gorillas and orangutans.
only the species Homo sapiens.
modern humans and extinct species more closely related to humans than to chimpanzees.

Hominins are the group consisting of modern humans and extinct relatives on the human lineage after its split from the chimpanzee lineage (e.g. Australopithecus, Homo erectus). Hominids include all great apes.
bio34a3-hev-6
Describe two skeletal features, other than the skull, that indicate a fossil hominin was bipedal, and explain how each is an adaptation for walking upright. (4 marks)

Valgus angle: the femurs angle inwards towards the knees, placing the feet under the body's centre of gravity for balance when walking; short, broad, bowl-shaped pelvis: supports the internal organs and provides attachment for muscles that stabilise the body on one leg during walking; (also accept S-shaped spine, which positions the centre of gravity over the hips and absorbs shock; or arched foot and non-opposable big toe in line with other toes, which act as a lever and absorb shock).
bio34a3-hev-7
Explain how mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) evidence has been used to support the 'Out of Africa' model of human origins. (3 marks)

mtDNA is inherited only through the maternal line and does not recombine, so changes accumulate only by mutation at a relatively constant rate; African populations show the greatest mtDNA diversity, indicating they are the oldest (more time to accumulate mutations); non-African populations carry a subset of African lineages, and molecular clock estimates trace all modern mtDNA to a common female ancestor in Africa, supporting a recent African origin and later migration.
bio34a3-hev-8
Explain why new fossil discoveries, such as Homo floresiensis on the island of Flores, can change scientists' understanding of human evolution. (2 marks)

Scientific models are based on available evidence, and the fossil record is incomplete; a new species with an unexpected combination of features (small brain and body, yet recent age and tool use) shows that several hominin species co-existed and that the human family tree is more branched than previously thought, so models must be revised.
vce-bio34-he-c1
A fossil skull has its foramen magnum positioned centrally underneath. This suggests that the species:
Walked on all fours
Walked upright (habitually bipedal)
Had a large brain
Used stone tools
A central foramen magnum balances the skull on a vertical spine. In quadrupeds it is towards the back of the skull.
vce-bio34-challenge: vce-bio34-challenge-1
A single-base deletion occurs in a gene. Where would it most likely have the greatest effect on the protein?
Near the end of the coding sequence
In an intron
Near the start of the coding sequence
It has the same effect anywhere
A deletion shifts the reading frame for every codon after it, so an early deletion changes almost every amino acid. Introns are removed before translation.
vce-bio34-challenge-2
Explain how STR profiling and gel electrophoresis can show whether a man could be a child's biological father.

STR regions are amplified by PCR and separated by size on a gel. A child inherits one allele at each STR locus from each parent, so every band in the child not from the mother must match a band of the biological father. One mismatch at several loci excludes him.
Mention PCR of STRs, separation by size, and the inheritance of one allele from each parent.
vce-bio34-challenge-3
An inhibitor binds to an allosteric site on an enzyme. Increasing the substrate concentration will:
Not restore the maximum rate, because the active site's shape has changed
Fully restore the maximum rate, because substrate outcompetes the inhibitor
Cause the inhibitor to break down, freeing the allosteric site again
Lower the activation energy further, partly making up for the inhibitor
Non-competitive inhibitors change the active site from elsewhere; more substrate cannot outcompete them.
vce-bio34-challenge-4
Light intensity is very low. Increasing the carbon dioxide concentration will most likely:
Greatly increase the rate of photosynthesis
Stop photosynthesis
Make little difference, because light is the limiting factor
Speed up the light-dependent stage
The rate is limited by whichever factor is in shortest supply. With little light, few ATP and NADPH are available for the Calvin cycle.
vce-bio34-challenge-5
Mitochondria are isolated from cells and placed in a solution with glucose and oxygen. Almost no ATP is produced because:
Mitochondria need light to produce ATP, just as chloroplasts do
Oxygen inhibits the Krebs cycle whenever glucose is also present
Glycolysis happens in the cytosol, so mitochondria cannot use glucose directly
Mitochondria can only respire fatty acids, not carbohydrates
Mitochondria take up pyruvate, not glucose. Supplying pyruvate would allow ATP production.
vce-bio34-challenge-6
A patient receives monoclonal antibodies against a virus. This gives:
Artificial active immunity, which is slower but long-lasting with memory cells
Artificial passive immunity, which is fast but short-lived with no memory cells
Natural passive immunity, like the antibodies passed on in breast milk
Natural active immunity, the same as recovering from the infection itself
The patient's immune system did not make the antibodies, so no memory cells form.
vce-bio34-challenge-7
An mRNA vaccine cannot change a person's DNA mainly because:
mRNA is too short to be read by ribosomes, so no protein is ever made from it in the cell
The mRNA stays in the cytoplasm, is translated, then broken down, and is never reverse-transcribed into DNA
The mRNA is made of DNA nucleotides, which cannot pair with the bases in the cell's own genes
The vaccine is destroyed in the bloodstream before it reaches any of the body's cells
The mRNA is translated by ribosomes into an antigen, then degraded; it does not enter the nucleus or become DNA.
vce-bio34-challenge-8
Influenza develops resistance to antivirals much faster than mammals evolve new traits. The main reasons are:
Viruses choose to change their genes when they detect an antiviral drug
Antiviral drugs cause the mutations that make the virus resistant
Viruses reproduce sexually, which mixes their genes every generation
A very short generation time, huge population sizes and a high mutation rate
Selection acts on variation each generation; many generations, many individuals and error-prone RNA replication mean resistant variants appear and spread quickly.
vce-bio34-challenge-9
Explain how one base substitution could have no effect, a small effect, or a large effect on a protein.

No effect: a silent mutation, because the genetic code is degenerate. Small effect: a missense mutation swaps one amino acid for a similar one or one away from the active site. Large effect: a nonsense mutation creates an early stop codon, or a missense change alters the active site.
Give a named mutation type and the reason for each outcome.
vce-bio34-challenge-10
Design a controlled experiment to test how temperature affects the activity of the enzyme catalase. Identify the independent and dependent variables and two controlled variables.

IV: temperature (for example 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 °C, using water baths). DV: rate of O₂ production (volume of gas or foam height per minute). Controlled: catalase concentration and volume, H₂O₂ concentration and volume, pH. Repeat each trial at least three times.
A good design states measurable variables, a range of values, controls and repetition.

X.title: Human insulin, from gene to bacteria
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Biology exam, Section B

pieces.text: Insulin is a protein hormone made by beta cells in the pancreas. The insulin gene is transcribed and translated, and the protein is then processed and exported from the cell.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Describe two differences between the structure of DNA and the structure of mRNA.
pieces.answer: Any two: DNA is double-stranded and mRNA is single-stranded; DNA contains deoxyribose and mRNA contains ribose; DNA contains thymine and mRNA contains uracil instead.

steps.working: First difference, for example: DNA is double-stranded, while mRNA is single-stranded.
Second difference, for example: DNA nucleotides contain the sugar deoxyribose and the base thymine, while mRNA nucleotides contain ribose and uracil.

pieces.mistake: Giving differences in function or location (such as 'DNA stays in the nucleus'). The question asks about structure.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Part of the template strand of a gene reads 3′ TAC GGA TTC 5′. Write the mRNA sequence transcribed from it, and the amino acids it codes for. Use these codons: AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, AAG = Lys.
pieces.answer: mRNA: 5′ AUG CCU AAG 3′; amino acids: Met–Pro–Lys

steps.working: The mRNA is complementary to the template strand, with U in place of T: 3′ TAC GGA TTC 5′ gives 5′ AUG CCU AAG 3′.
Read the codons in order from the 5′ end: AUG = Met, CCU = Pro, AAG = Lys, so Met–Pro–Lys.

pieces.mistake: Writing T in the mRNA, or copying the template strand instead of pairing with it. mRNA contains uracil and is complementary to the template strand.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Insulin is exported from the cell. Describe the path the insulin protein takes from the ribosome to the outside of the cell.
pieces.answer: It is made by ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum and enters the RER, travels in a transport vesicle to the Golgi apparatus where it is modified and packaged, then leaves in a secretory vesicle that fuses with the plasma membrane and releases it by exocytosis.

steps.working: Ribosomes on the rough endoplasmic reticulum make the protein, which moves through the RER and then in a vesicle to the Golgi apparatus, where it is modified and packaged.
A secretory vesicle from the Golgi apparatus moves to the plasma membrane, fuses with it and releases insulin by exocytosis.

pieces.mistake: Leaving out the vesicles or the order of organelles. Proteins move between the RER, the Golgi and the membrane inside vesicles.

pieces.text: To make human insulin in bacteria, a DNA copy of the insulin gene is made from insulin mRNA (complementary DNA, or cDNA). It is inserted into a plasmid that carries a gene for resistance to the antibiotic ampicillin.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain why the cDNA copy is used instead of the insulin gene taken directly from human DNA.
pieces.answer: The human gene contains introns. Bacteria cannot remove introns, but cDNA is made from mature mRNA, so it has no introns and the bacteria can express it correctly.

steps.working: Human genes contain introns, which are removed from pre-mRNA by splicing. Bacteria cannot splice, but cDNA is copied from mature mRNA, so it has no introns.

pieces.mistake: Saying bacteria 'cannot read human DNA'. The genetic code is universal; the problem is the introns.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain why the plasmid and the cDNA are cut with the same restriction enzyme, and name the enzyme that joins them together.
pieces.answer: The same enzyme gives both pieces complementary sticky ends, which base-pair with each other. DNA ligase then joins the sugar–phosphate backbones.

steps.working: Cutting both with the same restriction enzyme produces complementary sticky ends, so the cDNA and the plasmid can base-pair at the cut site.
DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones, sealing the gene into the plasmid.

pieces.mistake: Naming DNA polymerase. Ligase joins existing fragments; polymerase builds a new strand from nucleotides.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: After transformation, the bacteria are grown on agar containing ampicillin. Explain why only some bacteria form colonies, and why growing on ampicillin does not prove that a colony contains the insulin gene.
pieces.answer: Only bacteria that took up a plasmid have the ampicillin-resistance gene and survive. But a plasmid that closed up again without the insulin gene also gives resistance, so the colonies must be screened further (for example with a second marker gene or PCR).

steps.working: Transformation is inefficient: only bacteria that took up a plasmid carry the ampicillin-resistance gene, so only they survive and form colonies.
Plasmids that rejoined without the insert also carry the resistance gene, so a resistant colony may not contain the insulin gene; further screening is needed.

pieces.mistake: Assuming every resistant colony has the recombinant plasmid. Resistance only shows that a plasmid was taken up.

X.title: A new virus: immunity, vaccines and resistance
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Biology exam, Section B
