pieces.text: A newly identified respiratory virus has a protein, called S, on its outer surface. People infected for the first time take about a week to recover.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain how the S protein causes B cells that recognise it to multiply.
pieces.answer: S is an antigen: it is non-self and triggers an immune response. The few naive B cells whose receptors are complementary to S bind it (clonal selection) and, with cytokines from activated helper T cells, divide to form many identical plasma and memory B cells (clonal expansion).

steps.working: S acts as an antigen. Only the B cells with receptors (membrane-bound antibodies) complementary to S bind it, which selects them (clonal selection).
Helped by cytokines from activated helper T cells, the selected B cells divide into clones of plasma cells and memory B cells (clonal expansion).

pieces.mistake: Saying B cells 'make the right antibody' after meeting the antigen. The specific B cells already exist; the antigen selects them.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Describe two ways antibodies against S help to remove the virus.
pieces.answer: Any two: neutralisation (antibodies block S so the virus cannot attach to and enter host cells); agglutination (clumping virus particles together); opsonisation (marking virus particles for phagocytosis); activating complement proteins.

steps.working: First way, for example: neutralisation, where antibodies bind S and stop the virus attaching to host cells.
Second way, for example: agglutination or opsonisation, which clumps or tags virus particles so phagocytes engulf them more easily.

pieces.mistake: Saying antibodies 'kill' or 'destroy' the virus. Antibodies bind and mark it; other parts of the immune system remove it.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain why cytotoxic T cells are needed to clear an infection that is already established.
pieces.answer: Viruses replicate inside host cells, where antibodies cannot reach them. Infected cells display viral antigens on MHC class I markers; cytotoxic T cells recognise these and cause the infected cells to die (apoptosis), stopping the virus multiplying.

steps.working: Once inside host cells, the virus is out of reach of antibodies.
Infected cells present viral antigen on MHC class I markers; cytotoxic T cells recognise them and induce apoptosis in those cells.

pieces.mistake: Saying cytotoxic T cells attack free virus particles. They target infected body cells.

pieces.text: A vaccine containing harmless copies of the S protein is developed.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain how this vaccine gives long-term protection against the virus.
pieces.answer: The vaccine triggers a primary immune response that produces memory B and T cells specific to S (artificial active immunity). On later exposure to the virus, the memory cells give a faster and larger secondary response, so the virus is removed before it causes disease.

steps.working: The vaccine's S protein triggers a primary response, producing memory B cells and memory T cells specific to S.
If the virus is met later, memory cells produce a faster, stronger secondary response that clears it before symptoms develop.

pieces.mistake: Saying the vaccine gives the person antibodies. Antibodies from a vaccine fade; long-term protection comes from memory cells.

pieces.text: An antiviral drug blocks one of the virus's enzymes. A few years after the drug comes into wide use, a strain of the virus that is resistant to the drug has become common.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain how the resistant strain became common.
pieces.answer: A random mutation in the gene for the enzyme had already produced resistant virus particles before the drug was used. The drug acted as a selection pressure: it stopped susceptible particles replicating, while resistant ones survived and replicated. Over many generations the resistance allele became more frequent in the virus population.

steps.working: Variation: a random mutation in the viral gene for the enzyme produced resistant virus particles. The mutation was already present; the drug did not cause it.
Selection: the drug stopped susceptible particles replicating, but resistant particles survived and replicated, passing on the resistance allele.
Over many generations, the frequency of the resistance allele increased until the resistant strain was common.

pieces.mistake: Saying the virus 'became resistant because of the drug' or 'adapted to the drug'. Resistance comes from a random mutation that the drug then selects for.

X.title: Photosynthesis, Rubisco and a gene-edited crop
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Biology exam, Section B

pieces.text: Rubisco is the enzyme that fixes carbon dioxide in the light-independent stage of photosynthesis. It can also bind oxygen instead, a process called photorespiration that wastes energy and reduces the plant's output of glucose.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Name where the light-independent stage occurs, and the two products of the light-dependent stage that it uses.
pieces.answer: In the stroma of the chloroplast; it uses ATP and NADPH.

steps.working: Location: the stroma of the chloroplast.
Inputs from the light-dependent stage: ATP and NADPH.

pieces.mistake: Naming the thylakoid membranes (grana). They are the site of the light-dependent stage.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: On hot, dry days the rate of photosynthesis in C3 plants falls. Explain why.
pieces.answer: Stomata close to save water, so CO₂ falls and O₂ builds up inside the leaf; Rubisco then binds O₂ more often (photorespiration), so less carbon is fixed.

steps.working: The plant closes its stomata to reduce water loss, so CO₂ cannot enter and O₂ accumulates in the leaf.
With a higher O₂ to CO₂ ratio, Rubisco binds O₂ more often, increasing photorespiration and reducing carbon fixation.

pieces.mistake: Saying only that the enzyme denatures. The main effect at moderate heat is stomatal closure and photorespiration.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain how C4 plants reduce photorespiration.
pieces.answer: They first fix CO₂ into a 4-carbon compound in mesophyll cells, then release it in bundle-sheath cells, keeping CO₂ concentration high around Rubisco.

steps.working: In mesophyll cells, CO₂ is first fixed by an enzyme that does not bind O₂, forming a 4-carbon compound.
This compound is moved to bundle-sheath cells and releases CO₂ there, so Rubisco is surrounded by high CO₂ and rarely binds O₂.

pieces.mistake: Describing CAM plants, which separate the steps in time (night and day), not in space.

pieces.text: Scientists use CRISPR-Cas9 to edit a gene in a crop plant so that it tolerates drought better.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Describe the roles of the guide RNA and the Cas9 enzyme.
pieces.answer: The guide RNA is complementary to the target DNA and leads Cas9 to it; Cas9 then cuts both strands of the DNA at that site.

steps.working: The guide RNA has a sequence complementary to the target gene, so it binds there and directs Cas9 to the correct site (next to a PAM sequence).
Cas9 is an endonuclease that cuts both strands of the DNA at the target site.

pieces.mistake: Saying Cas9 finds the gene by itself. The guide RNA provides the specificity.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: Explain how cutting the DNA can change the gene.
pieces.answer: When the cell repairs the break, bases are often inserted or deleted, which can knock out the gene; or a supplied DNA template can be inserted.

steps.working: The cell repairs the double-strand break; errors in repair add or remove bases (disrupting the gene), or scientists supply a template so a new sequence is inserted.

pieces.mistake: Saying Cas9 inserts the new gene. Cas9 only cuts; the cell's repair process makes the change.

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Give one benefit and one concern of growing gene-edited drought-tolerant crops.
pieces.answer: Benefit: higher, more reliable yields in dry conditions. Concern: for example, effects on ecosystems or reduced genetic diversity if one variety is grown widely.

steps.working: A benefit, such as more reliable food production in drought, using less irrigation water.
A concern, such as reduced genetic diversity, unknown ecological effects, or unequal access for farmers.

pieces.mistake: Giving vague answers such as 'it is unnatural'. Name a specific biological, social or ethical issue.

X.title: Birds on two islands
X.source: Original question in the style of the VCE Biology exam, Section B

pieces.text: About two million years ago, a population of seed-eating birds colonised two islands separated by deep water. The birds rarely fly between them. Today the birds on the two islands are separate species.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain how the two species could have formed.
pieces.answer: The water was a geographical barrier that stopped gene flow. Different selection pressures, mutations and genetic drift changed allele frequencies differently on each island. Over time the populations became reproductively isolated, forming separate species (allopatric speciation).

steps.working: A geographical barrier (the sea) separated the populations, so there was no gene flow between them.
Different selection pressures (for example different seeds), new mutations and genetic drift changed allele frequencies differently in each population.
Over many generations the populations became reproductively isolated, so they could no longer interbreed: separate species.

pieces.mistake: Saying the birds changed in order to adapt to each island. Variation arises randomly; selection acts on it.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: A storm kills most of the birds on one island, at random. Name this event and explain its effect on the gene pool.
pieces.answer: A bottleneck effect (a type of genetic drift): the survivors carry only some of the original alleles, so genetic diversity falls and allele frequencies change by chance.

steps.working: Bottleneck effect, a form of genetic drift.
The small surviving population carries only a random sample of alleles, so genetic diversity decreases and allele frequencies shift by chance, not by selection.

pieces.mistake: Calling it natural selection. The storm killed birds at random, regardless of their traits.

pieces.text: The DNA sequence of one gene was compared in three bird species. The number of differences is shown below.

pieces.label: c.i
pieces.question: Which two species are most closely related?
pieces.answer: A and B

steps.working: A and B have the fewest differences (4), so they share the most recent common ancestor.

pieces.mistake: Choosing the pair with the most differences.

pieces.label: c.ii
pieces.question: Explain why the number of DNA differences can be used to estimate how long ago two species diverged.
pieces.answer: Mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate, so more differences mean more time since the species shared a common ancestor (a molecular clock).

steps.working: If mutations build up at an approximately constant rate, the number of differences acts as a molecular clock: more differences means a longer time since divergence.

pieces.mistake: Saying more differences mean the species are more advanced.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: A fossil bird is found in a rock layer between two layers of volcanic ash dated at 2.4 and 2.1 million years old. Estimate the fossil's age and name the dating methods used.
pieces.answer: Between 2.1 and 2.4 million years old; the ash layers are dated by absolute (radiometric) dating, and the fossil's position between them uses relative dating (the law of superposition).

steps.working: The fossil is between 2.1 and 2.4 million years old.
The ash layers are dated by radiometric (absolute) dating; the fossil's age comes from its position between them (relative dating, superposition).

pieces.mistake: Saying the fossil itself was radiometrically dated. Here its age comes from the layers around it.

X.title: Challenge: insulin from bacteria
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of the VCE Biology exam, Section B

pieces.text: Researchers want bacteria to produce human insulin. They extract mRNA for insulin from human pancreatic beta cells and make complementary DNA (cDNA) from it.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Explain why cDNA made from mRNA is used rather than the insulin gene cut from a human chromosome.
pieces.answer: Bacteria cannot remove introns. mRNA has already been spliced, so cDNA contains only the exons.

steps.working: Human genes contain introns that are removed by splicing in eukaryotes.
Bacteria lack splicing machinery, so cDNA (exons only) is needed.

pieces.mistake: Saying bacteria cannot read human DNA. The genetic code is universal.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Name the enzymes used to insert the cDNA into a plasmid, and describe the role of each.
pieces.answer: A restriction endonuclease cuts the plasmid (and the cDNA ends) to leave matching sticky ends; DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones.

steps.working: Restriction enzyme: cuts at a recognition site, giving complementary sticky ends.
DNA ligase: forms phosphodiester bonds to seal the DNA.

pieces.mistake: Saying ligase forms hydrogen bonds between bases.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Before cloning, the cDNA is amplified by PCR from 50 copies through 20 cycles. How many copies are produced, and what is the role of the primers?
pieces.answer: About 5.2 × 10⁷ copies; primers bind to each end of the target and give Taq polymerase a starting point.

steps.working: 50 × 2²⁰ ≈ 5.2 × 10⁷ copies.
Primers are short sequences complementary to the ends of the target, where DNA polymerase starts adding nucleotides.

pieces.mistake: Using 50 × 20 or 2 × 50²⁰.

pieces.text: The plasmid has an ampicillin-resistance gene and a lacZ gene containing the insertion site. Bacteria are treated to take up plasmids, then grown on agar containing ampicillin and X-gal.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: Explain how the researchers can identify colonies of bacteria that contain the recombinant plasmid.
pieces.answer: Only bacteria with a plasmid grow on ampicillin. Of those, white colonies have the insert in lacZ (recombinant); blue colonies have a plasmid without the insert.

steps.working: Ampicillin kills bacteria without a plasmid.
A plasmid without an insert has a working lacZ, which breaks down X-gal to give blue colonies.
The insert disrupts lacZ, so recombinant colonies are white and are selected.

pieces.mistake: Choosing blue colonies.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: In a beta cell, insulin passes through the rough endoplasmic reticulum and the Golgi apparatus. Describe the role of each, and explain why bacteria may need extra steps to make active insulin.
pieces.answer: Rough ER: ribosomes make the polypeptide, which is folded and transported. Golgi: modifies and packages it into vesicles for secretion. Bacteria have no ER or Golgi, so the chains may need to be folded and joined after extraction.

steps.working: Correct roles of rough ER and Golgi apparatus.
Bacteria lack these organelles, so post-translational processing must be done another way.

pieces.mistake: Saying bacteria have a Golgi apparatus.

X.title: Challenge: responding to a new virus
X.source: Original challenge question in the style of the VCE Biology exam, Section B

pieces.text: A new respiratory virus spreads through a town. Most people infected for the first time are ill for about a week; people infected a second time months later have few symptoms.

pieces.label: a
pieces.question: Describe one physical and one chemical barrier in the respiratory tract that can stop the virus entering cells.
pieces.answer: Physical: mucus traps particles and cilia sweep it away. Chemical: lysozyme in mucus, or antimicrobial secretions.

steps.working: A correct physical barrier and how it works.
A correct chemical barrier and how it works.

pieces.mistake: Naming the skin. The question asks about the respiratory tract.

pieces.label: b
pieces.question: Explain why cytotoxic T cells, rather than antibodies, are needed to clear virus from infected cells.
pieces.answer: Viruses replicate inside cells, out of reach of antibodies. Infected cells display viral antigen on MHC I, and cytotoxic T cells recognise it and trigger apoptosis.

steps.working: Antibodies cannot enter cells.
Cytotoxic T cells recognise antigen on MHC I and induce apoptosis.

pieces.mistake: Saying antibodies kill infected cells directly.

pieces.label: c
pieces.question: Explain why a second infection months later causes few symptoms.
pieces.answer: Memory B and T cells from the first infection recognise the antigen quickly, so the secondary response is faster and larger, clearing the virus before symptoms develop.

steps.working: Memory cells remain after the primary response.
The secondary response is faster and produces more antibodies.

pieces.mistake: Saying antibodies from the first infection last forever.

pieces.label: d
pieces.question: After a year, variants appear that antibodies from earlier infections bind poorly. Explain how these variants become common.
pieces.answer: Random mutations in the gene for the surface antigen produce variation. Variants that antibodies bind poorly infect more people and replicate more (a selective advantage), so their alleles increase in frequency over generations.

steps.working: Mutation creates variation in surface antigens.
Immune escape gives a selective advantage: more infection and replication.
The variant allele becomes more frequent over many generations.

pieces.mistake: Saying the virus mutates in order to escape.

pieces.label: e
pieces.question: R₀ for the virus is 4. Using 1 − 1/R₀, find the herd immunity threshold.

steps.working: 1 − 1/4 = 0.75, so 75% of the population.

pieces.mistake: Calculating 1/R₀ (25%).

pieces.label: f
pieces.question: Monoclonal antibodies are given to high-risk patients. Give one advantage and one limitation compared with vaccination.
pieces.answer: Advantage: immediate protection, useful for people who respond poorly to vaccines. Limitation: no memory cells, so protection fades; it is also expensive and may not bind new variants.

steps.working: A valid advantage.
A valid limitation.

pieces.mistake: Saying monoclonal antibodies give lifelong immunity.
